Parameters. The six parameters of the adopted model (

Model Selection and Validation): precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, switch probability, cue sensitivity and placement noise. The outcome of each model is the participant’s posterior mean, standardised within the analysed sample. Slopes are therefore in parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, which makes them comparable across parameters; the means and SDs of the standardisation are reported, so that every slope can be expressed in the units of the parameter.

Questionnaires. STICSA state, STICSA trait, IU, BDI and OCI totals, each z-scored within the analysed sample. Each questionnaire enters its own model, as in RQ2; the questionnaires are not adjusted for each other.

Instruction condition. Unordered factor with the two planned sum-to-zero contrasts C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3) and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding the questionnaire term is the slope averaged over the three conditions, and its interactions with the two contrasts describe how the slope depends on the condition.

For each parameter, questionnaire and sample, two linear models are fitted with one row per participant:y_{z} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{cond}}^\top \mathbf{c} + \beta_q\, q_z + \boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{cond} \times q}^\top \mathbf{c}\, q_z + \varepsilon \qquad \text{(condition × questionnaire model)}y_{z} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{cond}}^\top \mathbf{c} + \beta_q\, q_z + \varepsilon \qquad \text{(across-condition model)}

where \mathbf{c} holds the two contrast codes. In the first model, \beta_q is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes. In the second, the slope is pooled over participants, so that each condition contributes in proportion to its size.

Tested terms. Three terms are tested for each parameter and questionnaire: q_z in the across-condition model (1 numerator df), and q_z (1 df) and cond:q_z (2 df) in the condition × questionnaire model. Each term is tested with an F-test against the model without it, which with the sum-to-zero coding is the Type III test. The slopes within each condition, in the two condition groups (C1 and C2 together, C3) and the two planned contrasts between conditions are estimated with emmeans::emtrends and reported unadjusted.

Multiple testing. For each of the three terms, the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five questionnaires, separately for each parameter and sample (18 sets of five tests per sample). This mirrors the RQ2 models, in which the correction runs across the questionnaires within each model and term.

Distribution of the parameters and residuals. The posterior means of cue sensitivity and placement noise are bimodal within C1 and C2 and concentrated near the upper prior bound in part of the sample (cue sensitivity in C3, where the instructions state the cue offset of 70°, which the model represents as a value of 1; placement noise for participants with the most variable placements, whose estimates reach the bound of 50°), and precision weighting, belief momentum and the switch probability are right-skewed. tambi_rq3_parameter_table.py writes these distributions to parameter_descriptives.csv (quartiles, skewness and the number of estimates and posterior intervals at each prior bound, by sample and condition), and fig_rq3_0_parameter_distributions shows them. As a consequence, the residuals are not normal in most models. The three tested terms are therefore also tested with Wald F-tests based on a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance matrix (HC3; 

MacKinnon & White, 1985). The Shapiro-Wilk test of the residuals and the largest Cook’s distance are reported for every condition × questionnaire model.

Uncertainty of the estimates. The posterior mean treats each participant’s parameter as known. To carry the uncertainty of the estimates into the group-level analysis, both models are refitted on each of 100 posterior draws per participant, standardised with the mean and SD of the posterior means, and the coefficients are pooled with Rubin’s rules (

Rubin, 1987), with the degrees of freedom of 

Barnard & Rubin (1999). This treats the posterior draws as plausible values. The fraction of missing information shows how much of the variance of a pooled coefficient is due to the uncertainty of the participants’ estimates.

records.content: symptom_parameter_models_v4.py reported partial correlations, in which each questionnaire was adjusted for the other six scales, and regressions with a polynomial condition term. The present models enter one questionnaire at a time and use the planned contrasts of RQ2, so that RQ2 and RQ3 answer their questions in the same way. Associations found only after adjusting for the other scales (for example STICSA trait with the switch probability in run 12_10) are therefore not expected to reappear here.

Generated chapter

Written by tools/build_model_results.py from the files diagnostics/model_diagnostics.csv and diagnostics/*.png of run 12_10, which each R script writes through tambi_model_diagnostics.R. Do not edit by hand.

This chapter reports, for every fitted model of the current analysis set, the checks of the assumptions on which its tests rest. The models themselves are not changed by these checks.

Gaussian linear mixed models (lmer). Conditional residuals (observation minus fitted value including the random effects), standardised by the residual SD: QQ plot and histogram against the normal distribution; skewness and excess kurtosis (0 for a normal distribution); share of standardised residuals beyond ±3 (.0027 for a normal distribution); Shapiro-Wilk test on at most 5,000 residuals; residuals and √|residual| against the fitted values, with the Spearman correlation of |residual| and fitted value; ratio of the largest to the smallest residual SD of the three instruction conditions. Participant random effects: QQ plots and the smallest Shapiro-Wilk p over the random-effect terms. Fit: singular fit and convergence messages. Collinearity: largest variance inflation factor of the main-effect terms (interaction terms are left out because their variance inflation factors are inflated by construction).

Generalised linear mixed models (glmmTMB, binomial and beta). Raw residuals of these models have no reference distribution. Simulation-based quantile residuals are used instead (

Dunn & Smyth, 1996; as implemented in DHARMa, 

Hartig, 2022): the fitted model is simulated 250 times, and the residual of an observation is the randomised proportion of simulated values below it. Under a correct model they are uniform. Reported are the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of uniformity, the dispersion ratio (variance of the observations around the simulated mean relative to the same quantity in the simulations; 1 if the dispersion is reproduced) with its simulation p-value, and the share of observations outside all simulated values.

Linear models (lm, RQ3). QQ plot, residuals and √|standardised residual| against fitted values, Shapiro-Wilk test, Koenker’s studentised Breusch-Pagan test, and Cook’s distance per participant.

Screening thresholds. A model is flagged for inspection of its figure when |skewness| > 1, |excess kurtosis| > 3 or more than 1 % of standardised residuals lie beyond ±3 (residual shape); when |ρ(|residual|, fitted)| > .2, the residual SD ratio between conditions exceeds 1.5 or the Breusch-Pagan p < .01 (residual variance); when the quantile residuals deviate from uniformity (KS p < .01) or the dispersion test has p < .05; when a participant random effect deviates from normality (Shapiro-Wilk p < .01); when a variance inflation factor exceeds 5; when the largest Cook’s distance exceeds 0.5; and for singular fits and convergence messages. With several thousand observations, the Shapiro-Wilk and KS tests detect departures that are too small to matter, so that the decisive information is the size of the departure in the figures and in the skewness, kurtosis and dispersion values. The thresholds are conventions for screening and are not decisions about the models.

Instruction condition is an unordered factor coded with two planned sum-to-zero contrasts: C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3), structure explained (C3) against not explained (C1, C2), and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0), rules mentioned (C2) against not mentioned (C1). Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted; pairwise comparisons are Holm-adjusted.

Each model is fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires, z-scored within the analysed sample (q_z). For every pre-specified questionnaire term, the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five questionnaires; q-values below .05 are printed in bold. In the models with condition × questionnaire terms, the questionnaire term is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes; the across-condition models estimate the slope pooled over participants.

Generated chapter

This chapter is written by tools/build_model_results.py from the output files of tambi_rq3_models.R (run 12_10). Do not edit it by hand: changes are overwritten at the next pipeline run. Interpretation belongs in 

Results by Research Question.

Instruction condition is an unordered factor coded with two planned sum-to-zero contrasts: C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3), structure explained (C3) against not explained (C1, C2), and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0), rules mentioned (C2) against not mentioned (C1). Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted; pairwise comparisons are Holm-adjusted.

One linear model per parameter and questionnaire, one row per participant. The outcome is the posterior mean of the parameter, standardised within the sample, so that slopes are in parameter SDs per questionnaire SD; the means and SDs are in the table below. The condition × questionnaire model (y_z ~ cond * q_z) tests the slope averaged over the three conditions (q_z) and its condition dependence (cond:q_z); the across-condition model (y_z ~ cond + q_z) estimates the slope pooled over participants. For each tested term, the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five questionnaires, separately per parameter and sample; q-values below .05 are printed in bold. Two sensitivity analyses accompany every test of a questionnaire term: the same test with a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance (HC3), and the slope pooled over posterior draws (plausible values, Rubin’s rules), which carries the uncertainty of each participant’s estimate. Self-reported internalizing symptoms and mental health … ? The questionnaire battery comprised nine questionnaires. Anxiety was assessed using the german version of the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA; cite), with its state and trait scales. Intolerance of Uncertainty was measured with the german version of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IU-18; cite). Depressive symptoms were assessed with the german version of the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II). Obsessive compulsive behavior was tested by the german verion of the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory (OCI). … Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS) …  … the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) … …. the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS) …. ACE. …. EAT …. Total scores were z-scored across participants. For the analysis of in-task affect, an internalizing composite was formed as the mean of the z-scored totals of the STICSA trait scale, IU, BDI, OCI, the Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS), the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS).

WITHIN TASK AFFECT

To get a single net placement location estimate per trial and participant (net placement center), we calculated the circular mean of the positions of the placed mosquito nets (0–7 nets) per trial and participant. Angles were wrapped … to avoid …  Error is the absolute circular distance in degree(°) between the placement centre and the hidden-state target. As described above, the hidden-state target is the center of the von Mises distribution and thus contains no outcome noise, unlike the observed attack direction. Analyses of how net placement centers were updated across trials use the observed attack direction. To compare placements across the two color cues, each participant’s learned cue-2 offset was subtracted from cue-2 placements. The offset was estimated, per episode, as the difference between the circular mean placements for the two cues on regular trials from the fourth trial of the episode onward, and averaged across episodes.

Net placements around each event are indexed as follows. The event trial (t0) is the trial in which the mosquito nets were placed before observing that the direction of the mosquito attack has shifted. The net placement in the event trial thus reflects a pre-event baseline. The first net placement after the displaced mosquito attack is t+1. The first net placement after the next attack is t+2; it is the first net placement at which an oddball and an episode transition can be distinguished – for an oddball, the target angle at t0 equals the target angle at t+2; for an episode transition, the target angle at t+1 equals the target angle at t+2. The following placement is t+3. After a transition, error is computed relative to the target angle of the new latent state, and after an oddball relative to the unchanged target angle.

Net entropy is the Shannon entropy, in bits, of the net allocation of the 7 nets over the 32 positions. It is 0 bits when all nets are stacked on one position and 2.81 bits when they occupy seven different positions, so that higher values indicate a wider spread of net allocation within a single trial.

Latent-state model. Net placement behaviour was described with a computational model in which an agent infers which of two latent states is currently active and allocates its nets according to its prediction (reduced_agent_v3.py; full specification in 

The Inference Agent). The agent represents the attack direction for each colour cue in each latent state, with the second state rotated by an estimated angle (initialized at 120°) and the second cue offset from the first by a learned cue offset. Observed attack directions are modelled as a mixture of a von Mises distribution around the direction of the current state (concentration \kappa = 4) and an oddball component displaced by the rotation angle, with oddball probability \rho_{\text{eff}} = 0.10 \cdot \text{nr}. Before each outcome, the belief that the second state is active is propagated with the switch probability h; after the outcome, it is updated by Bayes’ rule and then shifted back toward its previous value by the belief momentum \text{bm}. The estimated directions are updated by a delta rule whose step is reduced when the outcome is attributed to the oddball component. For the allocation, the agent forms a predictive distribution over the 32 positions as a mixture of the two states, with weights that commit to the more probable state (logistic function of the predicted state probability with gain 3), shifts it by a random circular displacement with standard deviation \text{pn} (placement noise), raises it to the power 1 + \text{pw} and converts it into seven nets. Precision weighting (pw) also scales the concentration of the predictive distribution and the learning rate of the direction estimates, so that a higher value yields a narrower, more concentrated allocation.

The model has six free parameters with independent uniform priors: precision weighting (pw, 0.1 to 5), noise reactivity (nr, 0.1 to 3), belief momentum (bm, 0 to 0.95), switch probability (h, 0.005 to 0.30), cue sensitivity (cs, 0 to 1; the learned cue offset approaches cs × 70°) and placement noise (pn, 0 to 0.873 rad). Precision weighting determines how concentrated the nets are; noise reactivity, how strongly outcomes far from the expected direction are attributed to oddballs rather than to a change of state; belief momentum, how slowly the state belief follows new evidence; the switch probability, how readily a change of state is expected on any trial; cue sensitivity, how fully the offset between the two colour cues is learned; and placement noise, how variable the placements are around the predicted direction. All fixed constants are listed in 

Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants; the choice of the commitment gain is described in 

Model Selection and Validation.

Alternative models. Four alternative models were specified to test whether behaviour required latent-state inference (

Model Comparison): nets placed at random positions; a single direction tracked by a delta rule without distinguishing the colour cues; the same with a learned cue offset; and an agent that knows both directions of each cue and covers both on every trial without inferring which state is active.

Estimation. Parameters and model probabilities were estimated by amortized simulation-based inference with BayesFlow 2.0 (

Radev et al., 2023). Each session was summarized by 54 behavioural features describing the spread of the allocation, accuracy and interception, the trial-to-trial change of the placement, the responses to oddballs and episode transitions, and the use of the colour cues (feature_extraction_v3.py; 

Feature Extraction). The posterior network (flow matching with a summary network) was trained on 100,000 sessions simulated with parameters drawn from the priors on the 20 trial schedules of the study, for 150 epochs; for each participant, 4,000 posterior samples were drawn. The model classifier was trained on 100,000 sessions simulated from the five models in equal proportions, for 200 epochs, and returns the posterior probability of each model for a participant’s session.

Statistical analyses were conducted in Python (version) and R/RStudio (version).

Trial- and episode-level data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (LMM) fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in lme4 and lmerTest, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Proportions (beta distribution) and binary outcomes (binomial distribution) were modelled with generalized linear mixed models in glmmTMB (ref), tested with Wald z-tests. Model terms are reported as Type III F-tests.

Instruction condition was entered in every model as an unordered factor with two orthogonal, sum-to-zero planned contrasts. The first compares participants told the structure with those not told it (C3 versus the mean of C1 and C2, weights −1/3, −1/3, 2/3); the second compares participants told that rules exist with those told nothing (C2 versus C1, weights −1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding, all other terms of a model are evaluated as the unweighted mean over the three conditions. Condition differences are reported as contrasts of the estimated marginal means (emmeans package in RStudio; ref), which average over the covariates of a model. Model coefficients are reported instead for interactions of condition with trial-level predictors, where they equal the difference between the contrasted conditions in the effect of that predictor. Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted. All pairwise condition comparisons are reported with Holm correction.

Random effects followed the design of each model, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant predictors and, where events or episodes were nested within participants, random intercepts for these units. Where this structure produced a singular fit, it was reduced stepwise, first by removing the correlations between random effects and then by removing random slopes. The structure used is reported with each model. Because the diagnostics (section 1.5.4) showed heteroscedastic or heavy-tailed residuals and non-normal random effects for several models, every test of a linear mixed model was repeated with cluster-robust standard errors (bias-reduced CR2 estimator, clustered by participant, with small-sample-corrected Wald tests; 

Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018), which do not assume normally distributed or homoscedastic residuals or random effects.

For each model, pre-specified ‘main-interest’ terms (A and D, the questionnaire term of the across-condition form and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation form; B, the event type × placement × questionnaire term and its interaction with condition; C, the questionnaire × prediction error, questionnaire × state error and condition × questionnaire × state error terms) were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR), separately for each term, and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted. All p-values are two-sided.

hierarchy.lvl4: 1.5.1. The Effect of the Level of Instruction on Task Behavior
1.5.1. The Effect of the Level of Instruction on Task Behavior

records.content:
The effects of instruction condition on net placement behavior were estimated with six models:
To examine how … / the effect of instruction condition on the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, we estimated the model (M1):

log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + cue + oddball on the preceding trial × condition + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),

which was fitted at trial level. Because oddball trials … they were excluded from this model (t+1), such that the error describes …  The model contained a random intercept for participant, random slopes for within-episode position and episode index, as well as a random intercept for episode within participant.

To examine the degree to which participants stacked multiple nets in a single location or distributed them across multiple locations within a trial, we computed the circular variance of the (up to) 7 net positions, cv = 1 − R, where R is the length of their mean resultant vector (cv ∈ [0, 1]). The circular variance was bimodal: on most trials the nets were stacked on one or a few neighbouring positions (cv < 0.10), and on the others they were split between distant positions. Because no unimodal distribution described this (a beta mixed model of cv did not pass the diagnostics described in section 1.5.4), the outcome was whether the allocation of a trial was split, defined as cv > 0.15, which for two equal groups of nets corresponds to a separation of more than about 63°; the distribution of cv has its minimum between 0.10 and 0.15. Whether the allocation was split was modelled with a binomial generalized linear mixed model with logit link (M2):

split ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),

which was fitted at trial level. The planned contrasts were also computed for the thresholds 0.10 and 0.20.

Furthermore, we examined the magnitude of change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, and how this is modulated by instruction condition, the different types of event trials (oddballs, episode transitions and outcome omissions). The change of the placement centre (shift) was calculated as the circular distance between the cue-offset-corrected placement centres of consecutive trials, in degrees. Because the placement centre did not change on 4.4 % of the trials, a constant of 1° was added before the logarithm, as for the error in M1. The model (M3):

log(shift + 1) ∼ condition + oddball + transition + omission on the preceding trial + condition × (oddball + transition) + within-episode position + episode index + number of oddballs so far in the episode + episode length + (1 + oddball + transition | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).

… the model comprises fixed effects of instruction condition and each event type, as well as an oddball–transition contrast per condition to examine whether the differential reactivity to oddball events versus the differential reactivity to episode transitions varies across conditions. Regular trials are the reference category.

Next, we examined whether participants transfer an episode transition shift observed in one cue to the second cue in the first trial in which the second cue occurs in the respective episode. This cross-cue transfer  was operationalized as the angular distance between two placements for the cue shown second in a new episode (|I_e|): its actual placement at its first appearance, and the placement expected had its previous placement been rotated by the episode’s 120° shift. The previous placement is the circular mean of the last three placements for that cue in the preceding episode, and |I_e| = 0° indicates complete transfer. The model (M4):

|I_e| ∼ condition × (episode index + transition direction) + number of trials of the first cue before the first trial of the second cue + (1 + episode index + that number | participant)

included … fixed effects … interaction contrasts … random effects … random slopes … and was fitted at episode level, with one estimate per episode and participant.

To examine how overall mosquito defense performance differed between instruction conditions and across the session, we fitted a binomial mixed model of whether a net intercepted the mosquito attack (M5):

intercepted ∼ condition × episode index + within-episode position + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).

… fixed effect of the level of instruction (condition), episode index, as well as their interaction, to test whether how mosquito defense performance varies across episodes differs between instruction conditions.   … random effects … random slopes …

The net placement error relative to the true hidden target at t0 to t+3 was modelled separately for episode transitions and oddballs, to investigate differences in net placement error patterns around the different events. An interaction effect between condition and trial (t0:t+3) operationalized how net placement error patterns around events differed across instruction conditions. The model (M6) was fitted as:

log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × trial + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant:event),

with trial as a four-level factor (t0:t+3). Planned contrasts between conditions were computed at each placement.

Finally, we examined the effect of the level of instruction on the relative weighting of state error relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers. On each regular trial with an observed attack, the prediction error (observed mosquito attack direction – net placement centre) is the sum of two components known to the experimenter: the outcome noise (observed mosquito attack direction – hidden-state target) and the state error (hidden-state target – net placement centre). The change of the net placement centre from that trial to the next was modelled as (M7):

update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 + prediction error + state error | participant).

In this parameterization, the coefficient of the prediction error is the weight on outcome noise, i.e. on the irreducible stochasticity, and thus the irreducible component of the total uncertainty. The coefficient of the state error is the additional weight on state error (distance of the net placement to the hidden-state target) beyond the weight on noise; the estimate is zero for a learner that responds to every outcome alike. All angles were expressed in the participant’s own frame (after removing the learned cue offset), and pairs in which the next trial showed either cue were included. The update, the prediction error and the state error were entered in units of 10°, which leaves the weights unchanged and avoids a convergence warning that occurred with angles in degrees. Condition-specific additional weights were obtained as simple slopes with emtrends (ref), at pairs in which the next trial showed the same cue.

hierarchy.lvl4: 1.5.2 Models of the Questionnaire Score Associations
1.5.2 Models of the Questionnaire Score Associations

records.content:
To examine how internalizing symptoms modulate overall task performance and signatures of structural inference, we estimated four linear mixed-effects-models (A–D) per questionnaire scale (trait anxiety [STICSA-T], state anxiety STICSA-S], depressive symptoms [BDI-II], intolerance of uncertainty [UI-18] and obsessive compulsive behavior [OCI-R]). Model A asks whether questionnaire scores relate to overall performance, as a boundary condition for the remaining models. Model B asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the response to an episode transition differently than to an oddball, that is, to a displaced attack that does or does not signal a change of latent state. Model C asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the weighting of state error (i.e. angular error between the participant’s current placement and the hidden target angle) relative to outcome noise. Model D asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the transfer of an episode transition to the second (i.e. previously unseen within the new episode) color cue. Each model was fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires.
Each model was fitted in two forms. First, we fitted the models across instruction conditions, with the model containing the questionnaire but no condition × questionnaire interaction, so that the questionnaire slope is estimated from all participants, each condition contributing in proportion to its size. These models are estimated to examine whether a questionnaire is associated with the outcome irrespective of instruction (i.e. which information about the hidden structure was provided). Second, we fitted an extended form of this model, by adding the condition × questionnaire interactions. From these models, the questionnaire slopes were estimated in each condition, pooled over C1 and C2 (participants not told the structure), and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. In these moderation-form models, the questionnaire main effect is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes, in which the (current) 13 C3 participants count as much as the (current) 29 C2 participants, and it is therefore not used as the across-condition estimate.

To examine whether questionnaire scores are associated with overall task performance (Model A), we extended  M1 and M5 by the questionnaire (A1, error relative to the hidden-state target, A2, interception), with the questionnaire term added to the fixed effects of M1 and M5 and the same random effects (A1, A2, (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode)).

Whether questionnaire scores are related to differences in response to oddballs compared to episode transitions was examined across the first (t+1) and second (t+2) post-event trial. For each episode transition and each oddball, the net placements in  t+1 and t+2 entered the model,

outcome ∼ condition × event type × trial × questionnaire + (1 + event type | participant) + (1 | participant:event),

with event type (oddball, transition) and placement (t+1, t+2) coded −1/2 and +1/2. The outcome was net placement error relative to the hidden-state target (B1) or net entropy (B2). The three-way interaction event type × trial × questionnaire tests whether the association of the questionnaire with the change of the outcome from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs. From the model, the questionnaire slope was estimated for each event type and placement, together with its change from t+1 to t+2 for each event type and the difference between event types at each placement.

In B2, the random slope for event type produced a singular fit and was removed. Because the three-way interaction term varies within participants, B1 was refitted as a sensitivity model with uncorrelated by-participant random slopes for event type, trial and their interaction (reduced to event type and event type × trial where singular). For B2, these random slopes were estimated at zero, so that the sensitivity model reproduced the primary model. MOVE THIS PARAGRAPH TO RESULTS?

Furthermore, we examined whether questionnaire scores modulated the relative weighting of state error (net placement error relative to the hidden state target) relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers, using the model (Model C)

update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + questionnaire × prediction error + questionnaire × state error + condition × questionnaire × state error + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 | participant).

The questionnaire × prediction error term operationalized the effect of the questionnaire scores on the weight on outcome noise; the questionnaire × state error term operationalized the effect of questionnaire scores on the additional weight on state error. Condition-specific slopes of the additional weight on state error were computed as linear combinations of the fixed effects (lmerTest::contest). The model contains a by-participant random intercept; a sensitivity model added an uncorrelated by-participant random slope for the state error. The update, the prediction error and the state error were entered in units of 10°.

An extended version of the cross-cue transfer model (M4) described above to examine whether questionnaire scores differentially modulated cross-cue transfer across instruction conditions. The model was estimated (Model D) as

|I_e| ∼ condition × questionnaire + number of first-cue trials × questionnaire + condition × (episode index + transition direction) + (1 + episode index + number of first-cue trials || participant),

with the number of first-cue trials centred on its mean. The random-effect correlations were removed because the correlated structure was singular. The interaction between the number of first-cue trials after an episode transition and questionnaire score additionally tested whether questionnaire scores are associated with differences in cross-cue transfer for different numbers of consecutive observations of the first color cue after an episode transition. To assess the influence of single participants on the slope in C3, the moderation form was refitted leaving out each of the 13 C3 participants with questionnaire data in turn. hierarchy.lvl4: 1.5.3 Analyses of the computational model and its parameters
1.5.3 Analyses of the computational model and its parameters

records.content:
Model comparison. Each participant was assigned the model with the highest posterior probability. Participants for whom random placement had the highest probability were flagged for exclusion from the analyses of the parameters. Because the exclusion rule is not yet final, the analyses of questionnaire scores and parameters are reported both for all participants with questionnaire data and for the participants assigned the latent-state model. The classifier was validated on 5,000 new simulated sessions (1,000 per model) by its accuracy, the expected calibration error of its probabilities, and the posterior probability assigned to the generating model. Because only the latent-state model contains placement noise, the comparison was repeated with a second classifier for which the three directed alternative models received the same placement noise (same prior and implementation), trained and validated in the same way; this classifier was applied to all participants, both classifiers were applied to simulated sessions of both model sets, and the model frequencies in the sample were compared by random-effects Bayesian model selection (

Rigoux et al., 2014).

Validation of the parameter estimates. Calibration of the posterior network was tested by simulation-based calibration (

Talts et al., 2018) on 1,000 sessions simulated from the priors, with 1,000 posterior samples each, using the empirical distribution function of the rank of the true value and simultaneous 95 % bands (

Säilynoja et al., 2022). Parameter recovery was quantified on 500 further simulated sessions as the Pearson correlation between true values and posterior means, the slope of the posterior means on the true values, and the correlations between the estimate of one parameter and the true values of the others.

Posterior predictive checks. For each participant, the model was simulated with 100 posterior draws on the participant’s own trial schedule, and the 54 features were computed from each simulated session. For each feature, two quantities were computed across participants: the mean difference between the observed value and the median of the participant’s posterior predictive distribution, in units of the between-participant standard deviation of the feature, and the Spearman correlation between observed values and posterior predictive medians. The correlation was compared with the correlation expected if the model had generated the data, obtained by correlating one simulated session per participant with the median of the participant’s remaining simulated sessions. Bootstrap 95 % intervals were computed over participants (2,000 resamples).

Construct validity of the parameters. Each parameter was correlated across participants with the behavioural measures that follow from its definition (twelve pre-specified pairs; parameter_behavior_models_v4.py), for example precision weighting with the mean net entropy, cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset and placement noise with the variability of the placements within a latent state. The behavioural measures were computed from the participants’ data and not from the model. The direction of each correlation follows from the definition of the parameter, and the twelve one-sided tests were Holm-corrected as one set.

Questionnaire scores and parameters. The association of each of the five questionnaires with each of the six parameters was estimated with linear models at the participant level (tambi_rq3_models.R; 

Questionnaires and Model Parameters). The outcome was the posterior mean of the parameter, standardzied within the sample, and the questionnaire score was z-scored within the sample, so that slopes are expressed in parameter standard deviations per questionnaire standard deviation. As for the questionnaire models of RQ2, each model was fitted in two forms with the planned contrasts for instruction condition: an across-condition form,

parameter ∼ condition + questionnaire,

whose questionnaire slope is pooled over participants, and a moderation form,

parameter ∼ condition × questionnaire,

from which the questionnaire slopes were estimated within each condition, pooled over C1 and C2, and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. Terms were tested with F-tests against the model without the term (Type III with the sum-to-zero coding). For each parameter and questionnaire, three terms were tested: the questionnaire term of the across-condition model (1 numerator df), and the questionnaire term (1 df) and the condition × questionnaire term (2 df) of the moderation model. The p-values of each of these terms were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, separately for each parameter and sample (18 sets of five tests per sample), and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted.

The posterior means of several parameters were not normally distributed within conditions (section 2.3.5): cue sensitivity and placement noise were bimodal in C1 and C2 and concentrated near the upper prior bound in part of the sample, and precision weighting, belief momentum and the switch probability were right-skewed. The residuals of the moderation models were accordingly not normally distributed in 54 of 60 models (Shapiro–Wilk p < .05). The same three terms were therefore also tested with Wald F-tests based on a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance matrix (HC3; 

MacKinnon & White, 1985), which does not assume normal or homoscedastic residuals.

The posterior mean treats each participant’s parameter as known. To include the uncertainty of the individual estimates, both models were refitted on each of 100 draws from each participant’s posterior distribution, with the outcome standardized by the mean and SD of the posterior means. The questionnaire coefficient of the across-condition model and the questionnaire coefficient and the two condition × questionnaire coefficients of the moderation model were pooled over the 100 fits with Rubin’s rules (

Rubin, 1987), with the degrees of freedom of 

Barnard & Rubin (1999), and tested with t-tests. The fraction of missing information of a pooled coefficient is the share of its variance that is due to the uncertainty of the individual estimates.

Instruction effects on the parameters and on behaviour. The effect of instruction condition on each parameter was estimated with a linear model of the posterior mean (standardized within the sample) with the two planned contrasts; the contrasts were corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure over the six parameters, separately for each contrast and sample, and tested with HC3 standard errors as sensitivity analysis. To test whether the parameters describe the instruction effects found in RQ1, each RQ1 outcome was summarized per participant (mean log error relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials, proportion of intercepted attacks, proportion of split allocations, mean log shift after transitions and after oddballs minus after regular trials, mean |I_e|, and the participant estimate of the additional weight on state error from M7) and regressed, after standardisation, on condition alone and on condition and the six parameters. The planned contrast C3 versus C1 and C2 of the two models and the F-test of condition given the parameters show how much of the instruction effect on the behaviour is carried by the dimensions that the parameters describe. Because the parameters are estimated from the same behaviour, this is a test of description, not of mediation.

Incremental validity. For the association of a parameter with a questionnaire, a linear model of the questionnaire score (z) on condition and the behavioural measures that define the parameter (markers) was compared with the same model including the parameter (F-test of the parameter, 1 df; change of R²; HC3 sensitivity). For belief momentum, the markers were the change of the placement centre on the trials after an episode transition, the slope of the recovery of the error after transitions and the error on the first placement after a transition (the participant-level counterpart of the association of STICSA state anxiety in Model B1). Because each parameter is a function of all 54 summary features, incremental validity can only be tested against a selection of interpretable measures.

Reliability. The posterior reliability of each parameter was computed as the variance of the posterior means divided by the sum of this variance and the mean posterior variance, that is, the share of the between-participant variance of the estimates that is not estimation uncertainty. Split-half reliability is estimated by splitting each session at the episode boundary closest to its middle trial and estimating the parameters of each half with a posterior network trained on simulated full sessions whose features were computed from the same half (split_half_networks.py); each network was validated by parameter recovery on 500 simulated sessions, the correlation between halves was corrected with the Spearman–Brown formula (bootstrap 95 % intervals over participants, 2,000 resamples), and it was compared with the split-half reliability of one behavioural marker of each parameter computed from the same halves.

The assumptions of every fitted model were examined with the same procedure (tambi_model_diagnostics.R, called by each analysis script; all figures and values in 

Model Diagnostics). For the Gaussian linear mixed models, the conditional residuals (observation minus fitted value including the random effects) were inspected in QQ plots, histograms and plots against the fitted values, and summarized by their skewness, excess kurtosis and the share of standardized residuals beyond ±3; the homogeneity of the residual variance was assessed by the Spearman correlation of the absolute residuals with the fitted values and by the ratio of the largest to the smallest residual standard deviation of the three conditions. For the beta and binomial mixed models, whose raw residuals have no reference distribution, simulation-based quantile residuals were computed from 250 simulations of the fitted model (

Dunn & Smyth, 1996) and tested for uniformity (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) and for over- or underdispersion. For all mixed models, the predicted participant random effects were inspected in QQ plots and tested with the Shapiro–Wilk test, and singular fits, convergence messages and the variance inflation factors of the main-effect terms were recorded. For the participant-level linear models of the questionnaire and parameter analyses, the residuals were additionally tested for heteroscedasticity (Koenker’s studentized Breusch–Pagan test), and the influence of single participants was assessed by Cook’s distance. The diagnostics led to four changes of the models, each described with the model: the shift in M3 was log-transformed with a constant of 1° instead of 0.001; the outcome of M2 was changed from the circular variance to whether the allocation was split; and the angles of M7 and Model C were entered in units of 10°. For the remaining departures (heavy-tailed or heteroscedastic residuals, non-normal random effects), all tests of the linear mixed models were repeated with cluster-robust standard errors (section 1.5).

The change of mosquito net placements after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M3) of …. , (which also served as a manipulation check).

Participants thus responded to displaced mosquito attacks, and moved their net placement less after trials on which no mosquito attack had been shown (omission trials). With deeper instruction they moved more after episode transitions than after oddballs. The condition effects (level of instruction) on net placement error relative to the target angle (hidden-state target) after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M6), as planned contrasts of the condition means at each net placement. After episode transitions, the difference between conditions depended significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 1618) = 15.48, p < .001) – on the transition trial itself (t0), placed before the first attack of the new latent state, net placement error did not differ significantly between conditions (C3 versus C1 + C2, 0.16 log units, SE = 0.139, t(235.9) = 1.16, p = .247; C2 versus C1, −0.08, SE = 0.127, t(236.6) = −0.65, p = .517). From the first net placement after the episode transition onward, net placement error was significantly lower in C3 than in C1 and C2, by an amount that increased across trials.

The model-estimated mean net placement error was 3.98 (C1), 3.80 (C2) and 3.14 (C3) log units at t+1, 3.53, 3.36 and 2.39 at t+2, and 3.82, 3.63 and 2.48 at t+3. Descriptively, the net placement center at t+1 had moved 0.24 (C1), 0.29 (C2) and 0.61 (C3) of the 120° rotation toward the new latent state, and at t+2 0.34, 0.37 and 0.79. In all conditions, net placement error rose again from t+2 to t+3. This rise coincides with the first appearance of the other color cue after the episode transition, which carries higher error than a repeat appearance of the first color cue (supplementary analysis ADD).

After oddballs, the difference between conditions did not depend significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 2839) = 2.08, p = .052). Net placement error was lower in C3 than in C1 and C2 in every trial, including the oddball trial itself (t0, −0.81 log units, SE = 0.172, t(96.9) = −4.72, p < .001; t+1, −0.58, p = .001; t+2, −0.91, p < .001; t+3, −0.96, p < .001), and did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 in any trial (all p ≥ .093). Because oddballs occur within stable phases, in which C3 participants were more accurate, the C3 advantage after oddballs reflects their accuracy before the oddball rather than a different response to it.

The additional weight on state error (updating based on the hidden state target) compared to weight on noise was estimated with the weighting model (M7) described above. Condition-specific weights were obtained as simple slopes, and condition differences as planned contrasts of those slopes.

The additional weight on state error did not differ significantly from zero in C1 (0.07, SE = 0.095, t(60.9) = 0.72, p = .476), and it was significantly greater than zero in C2 (0.25, SE = 0.088, t(43.2) = 2.80, p = .008) and in C3 (0.66, SE = 0.184, t(658.0) = 3.56, p < .001). It was significantly greater in C3 than in C1 and C2 (planned contrast = 0.50, SE = 0.188, t(386.3) = 2.65, p = .008), and it did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 (planned contrast = 0.18, SE = 0.118, t(41.8) = 1.52, p = .137).

The weight on outcome noise was significantly greater than zero in C1 (0.37, SE = 0.094, t(57.8) = 3.87, p < .001) and C2 (0.30, SE = 0.088, t(41.6) = 3.36, p = .002), but not in C3 (0.08, SE = 0.181, t(562.3) = 0.44, p = .663). The planned contrasts of the weight on outcome noise were not significant (C3 versus C1 + C2, −0.25, SE = 0.185, t(334.3) = −1.36, p = .176; C2 versus C1, −0.07, SE = 0.118, t(39.8) = −0.58, p = .564).



Figure 4:Note.

Expressed as percentages, participants in C1 followed on average 37% of the outcome noise and corrected 43% of the state error, participants in C2 followed 30% and corrected 54%, and participants in C3 followed 8% of the noise and corrected 73% of the state error. The weight on outcome noise thus decreased descriptively with instruction, but only the additional weight on state error differed significantly between participants told and not told the structure. Participants in C1 corrected their error about the hidden state no more than they followed outcome noise, whereas participants in C3 corrected state error selectively.

For the paper --> table). With cluster-robust standard errors, the condition × questionnaire term was not significant for IU (F(2, 13.9) = 2.42, p = .125) or OCI (F(2, 6.6) = 4.03, p = .072). In C3, higher IU scores were significantly associated with higher net placement error relative to the hidden-state target (simple slope = 0.27 log units per SD, SE = 0.091, t(59.5) = 2.94, p = .005), as were higher OCI scores (0.30, SE = 0.110, t(59.6) = 2.73, p = .008) and higher STICSA trait scores (0.15, SE = 0.072, t(58.6) = 2.12, p = .038). In C1 and C2, the pooled slopes were close to zero for all three questionnaires (IU −0.01, OCI −0.02, STICSA trait −0.05, all p ≥ .34). The planned contrast between the slope in C3 and the pooled slope in C1 and C2 was significant for IU (0.27, SE = 0.100, t(59.5) = 2.73, p = .008), OCI (0.32, SE = 0.118, t(59.5) = 2.68, p = .009) and STICSA trait anxiety (0.20, SE = 0.089, t(58.8) = 2.29, p = .026). (THIS LAST RESULT THAT THE C1/C2 vs C3 contrast was significant for trait anxiety while the interaction with condition was not (with p = .075, so maybe simply underpowered) sounds counterintuitive in the first place and actually, maybe we should stick to reporting the planned contrasts only? Or briefly explain the difference)

(For scale, the accuracy advantage of C3 over C1 and C2 was 0.76 log units in M1, so that one SD on IU or OCI corresponded to a reduction of about a third of that advantage.)

The associations with mosquito attack interception were estimated with Model A2. In the across-condition form, no questionnaire was significantly associated with mosquito attack interception (largest slope, OCI, 0.11 log-odds per SD, SE = 0.067, z = 1.69, p = .091; all other p ≥ .13). In the moderation form, no condition × questionnaire interaction was significant (all p ≥ .34).

Participants with higher and lower questionnaire scores thus performed equally well when the structure had to be inferred. When it had been instructed, participants with higher IU and OCI scores, and to a smaller degree (SPECIFY) higher STICSA trait scores, were less accurate, but not less often successful in intercepting the mosquito attack.

records.content:
The associations of the questionnaires with the change of mosquito net placement error from the first to the second trial after an event were estimated with Model B1. The three-way interaction of event type × trial × questionnaire, tested whether the association of a questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs.

In the across-condition form, this interaction was significant for OCI (F(1, 1432) = 7.76, p = .005, q = .022), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 1416) = 6.92, p = .009, q = .022) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 1433) = 4.91, p = .027, q = .045), at the threshold for IU (F(1, 1422) = 3.84, p = .050, q = .063), and not significant for BDI (F(1, 1419) = 0.61, p = .435). For the two STICSA scales, the association of the questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2, averaged over event types, was also significant (trial × questionnaire, STICSA state F(1, 1433) = 8.92, p = .003; STICSA trait F(1, 1416) = 8.52, p = .004).

The simple slopes of the questionnaires show where this interaction arises. After episode transitions, net placement error decreased more steeply from t+1 to t+2 with higher STICSA trait scores (change of the slope = −0.25 log units per SD, SE = 0.072, t(1358) = −3.50, p < .001), STICSA state scores (−0.24, SE = 0.072, t(1361) = −3.28, p = .001) and OCI scores (−0.17, SE = 0.072, t(1361) = −2.32, p = .021), and not significantly with IU (−0.10, p = .18) or BDI scores (−0.11, p = .15). After oddballs, the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 was not associated with any questionnaire (STICSA trait −0.01, STICSA state −0.03, OCI 0.09, IU 0.08, BDI −0.03, all p ≥ .12).

The steeper decrease in net placement error after episode transitions for higher STICSA trait, STICSA state and OCI scores arose from higher net placement error at t+1. On the first placement after an episode transition, higher STICSA state scores were significantly associated with higher error relative to the new target (simple slope = 0.20 log units per SD, SE = 0.074, t(103.6) = 2.76, p = .007), and descriptively, higher STICSA trait (0.14, SE = 0.075, t(102.2) = 1.89, p = .062) and OCI scores (0.14, SE = 0.075, t(103.3) = 1.91, p = .059) showed the same tendency, but without reaching significance. At t+2, none of these slopes was significant (STICSA state −0.03, STICSA trait −0.11, OCI −0.02, all p ≥ .15). At t+1, the slope after episode transitions exceeded the slope after oddballs significantly for OCI (difference = 0.19, SE = 0.083, t(114.6) = 2.30, p = .023) and at the threshold (“AT THE THRESHOLD” IS WEIRD FOR p = .058 OR AT LEAST NOT BEST PRACTISE BUT I GOT STUCK FINDING A BETTER WORDING (for now)) for STICSA state anxiety (0.16, SE = 0.083, t(114.0) = 1.91, p = .058). After oddballs, the slopes at t+1 were close to zero for all questionnaires (between −0.05 and 0.05, all p ≥ .47).

In the sensitivity form with by-participant random slopes for event type, placement and their interaction, the focal interaction remained significant for STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 69.3) = 5.59, p = .021) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 69.1) = 5.19, p = .026), and was at the threshold (SEE ABOVE) for IU (F(1, 67.9) = 3.86, p = .054) and OCI (F(1, 68.9) = 3.57, p = .063). With cluster-robust standard errors, the event type × trial × questionnaire term of the across-condition form remained significant for STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 22.0) = 7.57, p = .012), STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 16.7) = 6.24, p = .023) and OCI (F(1, 15.6) = 5.61, p = .031; q = .052 for all three), and was not significant for IU (p = .106).

In the moderation form, the four-way interaction (i.e. the three-way interaction described above + questionnaire as a fourth term; condition × event type × trial × questionnaire) did not depend significantly on instruction condition for any questionnaire (condition × event type × trial × questionnaire, all F(2, ≈1410) ≤ 0.81, all p ≥ .44). For STICSA trait anxiety, the difference between episode transitions and oddballs in the change of the slope from t+1 to t+2 was of the same size in C1 and C2 (−0.24, SE = 0.119, t(1416) = −2.04, p = .042) as in C3 (−0.25, SE = 0.166, t(1392) = −1.53, p = .127), and the same held for STICSA state anxiety (C1 and C2, −0.30, p = .020; C3, −0.23, p = .30) (NOTE. NOTICE THE DIFFERENCES IN P VALUES WHICH ARE LIKELY DUE TO SAMPLE SIZE DIFF. EFFECT COULD REACH SIGNIFICANCE AT (MUCH) LARGER N). For OCI, it (SPECIFY) was present in C1 and C2 (−0.25, SE = 0.101, t(1417) = −2.49, p = .013) and smaller in C3 (−0.15, p = .56), without a significant difference between them (p = .71).



Figure 5:Note.

Descriptively, the division of the nets between the two directions showed the same delay (Fig. X). On the first placement after an epsisode transition, participants in the lowest tertile of STICSA state scores already placed a larger mean share of their nets within one position of the new direction than of the old direction (0.36 versus 0.25). Participants in the highest tertile did not (0.26 versus 0.31). On the second placement, both tertiles placed 0.38–0.40 of their nets at the new direction and about 0.20 at the old direction. These values are descriptive; no statistical tests were computed on these descriptive differences.

Across individual episode transitions, about a third of net placements in the first trial after the respective episode transition (t+1) had no net at the new direction in either tertile, and net placements with all or nearly all nets at the new direction were less frequent in the highest tertile. The higher error at t+1 therefore reflects fewer nets moved (placed at?)  to the new direction, rather than a net placement at an intermediate direction.



Figure 6:Note.

Two further patterns in the moderation form were not part of the analyses based on the interaction terms (SPECIFY). First, the association of the questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 differed between conditions for OCI (condition × trial × questionnaire F(2, 1416) = 8.49, p < .001), BDI (F(2, 1410) = 5.22, p = .005) and STICSA trait anxiety (F(2, 1408) = 4.74, p = .009). These interactions were carried by the contrast between C2 and C1. In C2 relative to C1, higher scores were associated with a steeper decrease of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 after oddballs (C2 versus C1, STICSA trait −0.39, p = .008; BDI −0.37, p = .013; OCI −0.28, p = .024; STICSA state −0.33, p = .034) and, for BDI and OCI, also after episode transitions (BDI −0.41, p = .036; OCI −0.40, p = .013). Second, in C3, net placement error after oddballs increased from t+1 to t+2 with higher IU (change of the slope = 0.27 log units per SD, SE = 0.132, t(1510) = 2.07, p = .038) and OCI scores (0.32, SE = 0.157, t(1518) = 2.07, p = .039), but not with STICSA or BDI scores (all p ≥ .68).

Participants with higher STICSA and OCI scores thus placed the mosquito nets further from the new target on the first trial after an episode transition and fully closed this gap by the second trial, whereas their net placement locations (relative to the target) after an oddball did not differ. This pattern was present irrespective of instruction for the STICSA scales. Where the structure had been instructed, participants with higher IU and OCI scores moved further from the target in the placement after an oddball, consistent with their higher net placement error in C3 in Model A1.

The associations of the questionnaire scores (ACTUALLY, MAYBE “INTERNALIZING SYMPTOMS” OR SMTH LIKE THAT INSTEAD OF QUESTIONNAIRE SCORES COULD BE BETTER?) with net entropy after events were estimated with Model B2 (SPECIFY). In the across-condition form, the event type × trial × questionnaire interaction was significant for OCI (F(1, 1405) = 8.26, p = .004, q = .021), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 1395) = 6.10, p = .014, q = .034) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 1407) = 4.42, p = .036, q = .060), and not significant for IU (F(1, 1399) = 3.01, p = .083) or BDI (F(1, 1397) = 0.50, p = .48). The residuals of this model had heavier tails than the normal distribution (section 2.4); with cluster-robust standard errors, the interaction remained significant for OCI (F(1, 15.9) = 11.11, p = .004, q = .021), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 22.0) = 7.97, p = .010, q = .025) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 16.8) = 5.44, p = .032, q = .054).

For STICSA trait anxiety and OCI, the interaction arose at t+1. On the first placement after an event, higher scores were associated with a wider allocation after oddballs than after episode transitions (difference of the slopes, transition minus oddball, STICSA trait −0.054 bits per SD, SE = 0.025, t(2213) = −2.21, p = .027; OCI −0.052, SE = 0.025, t(2216) = −2.12, p = .034). At t+2, this difference was absent (STICSA trait 0.006, p = .80; OCI 0.019, p = .45), because the allocation after episode transitions widened from t+1 to t+2 with higher OCI scores (change of the slope = 0.048 bits per SD, SE = 0.020, t(1357) = 2.43, p = .015) and, at the threshold, higher STICSA trait scores (0.034, SE = 0.019, t(1356) = 1.73, p = .084).
STICSA state anxiety showed a different pattern. Higher state scores were associated with a wider allocation at both placements and after both events (simple slopes between 0.10 and 0.13 bits per SD; oddball t+1, 0.13, SE = 0.048, t(66.4) = 2.72, p = .008; transition t+2, 0.13, SE = 0.050, t(78.5) = 2.64, p = .010; transition t+1, 0.10, p = .057; oddball t+2, 0.11, p = .022).

In the moderation form, the difference between oddballs and episode transitions at t+1 was present in C1 and C2 for STICSA trait anxiety (−0.098 bits per SD, SE = 0.033, t(2211) = −3.00, p = .003), OCI (−0.065, SE = 0.028, t(2212) = −2.33, p = .020) and IU (−0.056, SE = 0.027, t(2212) = −2.05, p = .040), and close to zero in C3 (STICSA trait 0.006, OCI 0.040, IU 0.046, all p ≥ .43). The planned contrast between C3 and C1 + C2 was not significant (STICSA trait 0.10, p = .066; OCI 0.10, p = .17; IU 0.10, p = .12), and the four-way interaction was not significant for any questionnaire (all p ≥ .51).

After a single displaced mosquito attack, participants with higher STICSA trait, OCI and, in C1 and C2, IU scores thus spread their nets more widely when the mosquito attack was an oddball than when it was an episode transition. After an episode transition, their allocation on the first trial after the respective epsidoe transition (t+1) was not wider than that of participants with lower scores, and it widened on the second trial (t+2). Participants with higher STICSA state scores spread their nets more widely after both kinds of event.

The associations of the questionnaires with the weights on state error (net placement error relative to the hidden state target) relative to outcome noise (von Mises noise around the hidden state target) were estimated with Model C (SPECIFY). In the across-condition form, higher OCI and STICSA state scores were significantly associated with a lower weight on outcome noise (questionnaire × prediction error coefficient, OCI −0.091 per SD, SE = 0.028, t(8264) = −3.20, p = .001, q = .007; STICSA state −0.088, SE = 0.030, t(8267) = −2.93, p = .003, q = .009). The associations for STICSA trait anxiety (−0.047, p = .13), IU (−0.049, p = .14) and BDI (−0.038, p = .26) were in the same direction but did not reach significance.

Higher scores on four questionnaires were significantly associated with a greater additional weight on state error (questionnaire × state error coefficient, STICSA trait 0.096 per SD, SE = 0.032, t(8266) = 3.02, p = .003, q = .006; OCI 0.093, SE = 0.028, t(8252) = 3.27, p = .001, q = .005; STICSA state 0.077, SE = 0.030, t(8266) = 2.55, p = .011, q = .018; IU 0.069, SE = 0.033, t(8266) = 2.09, p = .037, q = .046). The association for BDI was in the same direction but did not reach significnance (0.043, SE = 0.034, p = .20).

In the moderation form, the association with the additional weight on state error depended significantly on condition for OCI (condition × questionnaire × state error F(2, 8254) = 10.70, p < .001, q < .001), IU (F(2, 8257) = 8.87, p < .001, q < .001), BDI (F(2, 8194) = 4.98, p = .007, q = .012) and STICSA trait anxiety (F(2, 8183) = 4.63, p = .010, q = .012), and not significantly for STICSA state anxiety (F(2, 8077) = 2.68, p = .069).

In C1 and C2, where the structure had to be inferred, higher symptom load was thus associated with a greater additional weight on state error for STICSA trait anxiety, OCI, IU and STICSA state anxiety. In C3, none of these slopes was significant, and the slopes for IU and OCI were negative. For scale, one SD on STICSA trait anxiety or OCI corresponded to an additional weight on state error of about 0.10 in C1 and C2, about half the difference between C2 and C1 (0.18) and about a fifth of the difference between C3 and C1 + C2 (0.50).

In the sensitivity model with an uncorrelated by-participant random slope for the state error (participant SD of the slope ≈ 0.22), the association of OCI with a lower weight on outcome noise remained significant (−0.074, t(8265) = −2.32, p = .020). With cluster-robust standard errors (CR2, clustered by participant), none of the questionnaire terms of the primary model was significant (all p ≥ .23); the participant-level questionnaire scores are tested against the trial-level variation of the updates in the primary model (about 8,250 residual df), so that its tests assume that the weights do not vary between participants beyond condition and questionnaire (MOVE TO LIMITATIONS?).

Participants with higher anxiety-related scores thus followed outcome noise less and, where the structure had to be inferred, corrected state error more, so that their weighting in C1 and C2 lay closer to that of participants told the structure. Where the structure had been instructed, higher IU and OCI scores were not associated with a greater weight on state error (ADD ANXIETY).

Associations with |I_e| were estimated with Model D. In the across-condition form, higher OCI scores were significantly associated with larger |I_e|, that is, with less transfer of the hidden-state change (i.e. the episode transition with it’s 120° environment shift) to the second cue (6.3° per SD, SE = 2.92, t(61.1) = 2.16, p = .035, q = .17). Descriptively, STICSA trait anxiety showed the same tendency (5.0°, SE = 2.94, t(61.3) = 1.70, p = .094), without reaching significance. STICSA state anxiety, IU and BDI were not associated with |I_e| (all p ≥ .36). With cluster-robust standard errors, the association with OCI was of similar strength (F(1, 15.3) = 4.71, p = .046, q = .13).

In the moderation form, the association did not depend significantly on condition for any questionnaire (condition × questionnaire, IU F(2, 59.2) = 2.29, p = .110; BDI F(2, 60.0) = 2.15, p = .125; OCI, STICSA trait and STICSA state, all p ≥ .36). In C3, the simple slope was positive for IU (13.7° per SD, SE = 6.97, t(58.9) = 1.96, p = .055) and OCI (16.9°, SE = 8.27, t(58.8) = 2.04, p = .046), and the planned contrast between C3 and C1 + C2 showed a trend for IU (14.4°, SE = 7.69, t(59.0) = 1.88, p = .065) and was not significant for OCI (12.5°, p = .16). In C1 and C2, the pooled slopes were close to zero (IU −0.8°, OCI 4.3°, both p ≥ .19). For BDI, the slope was larger in C2 than in C1 (C2 versus C1, 16.3°, SE = 7.97, t(60.0) = 2.05, p = .045), with slopes of opposite sign in the two conditions (C1 −9.3°, C2 7.0°, both p ≥ .14).

When each of the 13 C3 participants with questionnaire data was left out in turn, the C3 slope remained positive in every refit, ranging from 7.7° to 17.2° per SD for IU and from 6.6° to 23.3° for OCI. Its significance varied with the omitted participant (IU, p = .021 to .343; OCI, p = .009 to .614). (CAN BE REMOVED WITH HIGHER N)
Descriptively, |I_e| in C1 and C2 was distributed around the 90° expected for random net placement across the whole range of IU scores (Fig. 4a). In C3, participants with lower IU scores showed |I_e| of about 35°–55°, whereas participants with the highest scores showed |I_e| at or above 90°, the level of the uninstructed conditions (Fig. 4b).

Higher OCI scores were thus associated with less transfer of the change to the second cue across conditions, and higher IU and OCI scores with less transfer in C3, where the structure had been instructed. The C3 estimates rest on 13 participants and depend on individual participants (ATM).

The posterior probabilities of the five models were estimated for each of the 68 participants with the model classifier. The latent-state model had the highest posterior probability for 59 participants (87 %; C1, 21 of 24; C2, 25 of 30; C3, 13 of 14), random placement for 5 participants (7 %) and the model that covers both directions of each cue without inferring the active state for 4 participants (6 %). Neither of the two models that track a single direction had the highest probability for any participant (largest posterior probability of any participant below 10⁻⁸). For 66 participants, the highest posterior probability exceeded .99; for the remaining two, random placement was more probable than the latent-state model (.65 versus .35 and .82 versus .18).

On 5,000 simulated sessions, the classifier assigned 4,999 to the model that had generated them (accuracy 0.9998), and the expected calibration error of its probabilities was below 0.001 for every model. Its probabilities lie almost exclusively near 0 and 1, so that this validation shows that the five models can be separated on the 54 features when one of them generated the data. It does not show which of them comes closest to data that none of them generated. Of the five models, only the latent-state model contains placement noise and cue sensitivity. A sensitivity analysis in which the alternative models receive the same placement noise is implemented and has not yet been run (ADD RESULT; see 

Model Comparison).

records.content:
Calibration and recovery were evaluated on sessions simulated from the priors. In simulation-based calibration with 1,000 sessions, the rank distribution of the true value within the posterior remained inside the simultaneous 95 % band for all six parameters; the mean ranks deviated from their expected value by at most 1.4 standard errors, and the central 50 %, 80 % and 95 % posterior intervals contained the true value in 48 % to 50 %, 78 % to 82 % and 94 % to 96 % of the sessions. The posterior distributions were therefore neither systematically shifted nor too narrow or too wide.

Across 500 simulated sessions, the posterior means correlated with the true values at r = .998 for precision weighting, .988 for placement noise, .926 for belief momentum, .922 for cue sensitivity, .917 for the switch probability and .785 for noise reactivity. The slope of the posterior means on the true values was 0.82 to 0.99 for five parameters and 0.59 for noise reactivity, whose estimates are drawn toward the centre of the prior. In the range of precision weighting in which the participants’ estimates lie (1.5 to 3.5), the correlation for noise reactivity was .86 (206 sessions). The estimate of one parameter correlated with the true value of another at most at |r| = .21 (between noise reactivity and belief momentum). Within the posterior distributions, noise reactivity and belief momentum were negatively correlated (mean r = −.64), so that for a single participant a higher value of one is partly exchangeable for a lower value of the other.

records.content:
The model was simulated with 100 posterior draws per participant on the participant’s own trial schedule, and the 54 features of the simulated sessions were compared with the observed features of the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model (

Posterior Predictive Checks). For the 30 features that describe the level of a behaviour (means, rates and proportions), the mean difference between observed and predicted values had a median of 0.30 between-participant standard deviations, and the median Spearman correlation between observed and predicted values across participants was .76, which is 86 % of the correlation expected if the model had generated the data (median .91). The mean net entropy (ρ = .96; expected .97), the mean error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .92; expected .95), the proportion of intercepted attacks (ρ = .86; expected .93), the mean change of the placement centre from one trial to the next (ρ = .96; expected .96), the variability of the placements within a latent state (ρ = .92; expected .96) and the learned cue offset (ρ = .77; expected .89) were reproduced in this way. The fitted model therefore reproduced the differences between participants in the behaviours from which its parameters are estimated.

Two kinds of features were reproduced less well. The trial-to-trial variability of the behaviour, such as the standard deviation of the change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, was higher in participants than predicted by 1.0 to 1.7 between-participant standard deviations (four of five such features), while the ordering of participants was reproduced in part (ρ = .12 to .62). Differences, ratios and slopes, such as the change of the proportion of intercepted attacks over the session, were reproduced in value (median difference 0.57 standard deviations) but only partly in the ordering of participants (median ρ = .27, at 46 % of the expected correlation of .70). Within conditions, the rank correlations of the level features reached a median of 91 % (C1) and 88 % (C2) of the correlation expected within the same condition, but 63 % in C3 (13 participants), although the expected correlation was as high in C3 as in C1 and C2 (median .90); the largest differences concerned the error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .55, expected .86), the proportion of large changes of the placement centre (.46, expected .92) and the learned cue offset (.53, expected .88). A trial-level comparison located the first deviation: participants alternated between precise placements and discrete moves of the placement centre to the direction of the other latent state or to the location of a preceding oddball, which the model represents as a random displacement of the allocation on every trial (

Model Selection and Validation). Accordingly, the median error of the placement centre relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials was reproduced (median difference −0.5°), whereas its 90th percentile was higher in participants than predicted (median difference 29°; higher for 93 % of participants).



Figure 9:Mean difference between observed and predicted values of the 54 features, in between-participant standard deviations, with 95 % bootstrap intervals (59 participants).



Figure 10:Spearman correlation across participants between observed and predicted values of each feature (points, 95 % bootstrap intervals), and the correlation expected if the model had generated the data (vertical marks).

records.content: The posterior means of the parameters were correlated with the behavioural measures that follow from their definitions (68 participants; one-sided tests, Holm-corrected over the twelve pairs). Precision weighting correlated with lower mean net entropy (r = −.89, p < .001), a higher proportion of trials with stacked nets (r = .63, p < .001) and lower circular variance of the net positions (r = −.32, p = .004). Placement noise correlated with the variability of the placement centre within a latent state (r = .95, p < .001), and cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset (r = .71, p < .001), but not with the proportion of episodes in which the first placement for the second cue was closer to the new than to the previous direction (r = .05, p = .35). Belief momentum correlated with a smaller change of the placement centre after episode transitions (r = −.37, p < .001) but not with the slope of the recovery of the error after transitions (r = −.05, p = .34). The switch probability correlated with a steeper decrease of |I_e| with the number of preceding first-cue trials (r = −.31, p = .005) and, without surviving the correction, with the proportion of episodes in which the first placement for the second cue was closer to the new direction (r = .27, p = .013). Noise reactivity did not correlate significantly with the size of the change of the placement after oddballs (r = −.15, p = .11) or with its ratio to the change on regular trials (r = −.19, p = .061). All p-values are one-sided. Five of the six parameters were thus associated with at least one behavioural measure of the process they describe, in the direction implied by their definition; for noise reactivity, the correlations had the expected sign but did not reach significance.
