records.content:
Figure 11 shows the posterior mean and the 95 % posterior interval of each of the 68 participants by condition; the numbers below refer to the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model (parameter_descriptives.csv lists them for both samples). Median estimates (interquartile range) were 2.20 (1.86 to 2.69) for precision weighting, 1.00 (0.40 to 2.44) for noise reactivity, 0.20 (0.14 to 0.42) for belief momentum, 0.076 (0.035 to 0.133) for the switch probability, 0.84 (0.24 to 0.90) for cue sensitivity and 0.55 (0.25 to 0.77) rad for placement noise. The 95 % posterior intervals spanned a median of 8 % (precision weighting), 15 % (placement noise), 30 % (cue sensitivity), 34 % (switch probability), 37 % (noise reactivity) and 39 % (belief momentum) of the prior range. The posterior reliability of the estimates (variance of the posterior means relative to this variance plus the mean posterior variance) was 0.98 for precision weighting and placement noise, 0.92 for cue sensitivity, 0.88 for noise reactivity and the switch probability, and 0.82 for belief momentum; within C3, it was lower for noise reactivity (0.55) and cue sensitivity (0.53), whose estimates varied little between C3 participants.

The split-half reliability was estimated from the first and the second half of each session (split at the episode boundary closest to the middle trial), with a posterior network trained for each half. From half sessions, parameter recovery on simulated sessions reached r = .996 to .997 for precision weighting, .977 for placement noise, .88 to .91 for cue sensitivity and belief momentum, .86 to .90 for the switch probability and .71 to .72 for noise reactivity (first and second half). In the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model, the Spearman–Brown corrected correlations between the halves (95 % bootstrap intervals) were 0.86 [0.74, 0.93] for precision weighting, 0.82 [0.69, 0.92] for cue sensitivity, 0.74 [0.55, 0.86] for placement noise, 0.73 [0.56, 0.85] for belief momentum, 0.72 [0.54, 0.84] for noise reactivity and 0.52 [0.14, 0.73] for the switch probability. For comparison, the behavioural marker of each parameter reached 0.88 (mean net entropy), 0.76 (learned cue offset), 0.70 (variability of the placements within a latent state), 0.37 (slope of the recovery after transitions), 0.27 (ratio of the shift after oddballs to the shift on regular trials) and 0.73 (rate of switches without an event). Belief momentum and noise reactivity were thus considerably more reliable than the behavioural measures of the same processes, whereas the switch probability was less reliable than its marker. Precision weighting (median 2.04 versus 2.38, Wilcoxon p < .001) and belief momentum (0.21 versus 0.35, p = .005) were higher in the second half; the correlations between halves are therefore lower bounds of the reliability of a stable trait.

The distributions of the posterior means were not normal, for reasons that follow from the instructions and from the definitions and prior ranges of the parameters.

Cue sensitivity. In the model, the believed offset between the attack directions for the two colours approaches cue sensitivity × 70°, so that a value of 1 corresponds to the true offset of the task and any learned offset of 70° or more is represented by values near 1. Participants in C3 were told that attacks for one colour are offset by about 70° from those for the other, with an illustration adapted to their own trial schedule. All 13 of them had posterior means between 0.84 and 0.99 (median 0.96), and their observed learned cue offset had a median of 73°. Participants in C1 and C2 received no information on the colours, and their posterior means were bimodal: 23 of 46 had values above 0.7 and 18 below 0.3 (C1, 9 and 10 of 21; C2, 14 and 8 of 25), with observed learned cue offsets of 75° and 30° (medians), respectively. In the latent-state sample, the 95 % posterior interval reached the upper bound for 27 participants (C3, 10 of 13), so that differences between participants with offsets at or above the true offset are not resolved by this parameter.

Placement noise. Placement noise was lower in C3 (median 0.18 rad, 10°; 12 of 13 below 0.4 rad) than in C1 and C2 (0.62 and 0.65 rad), where the distribution was again bimodal (13 of 46 participants below 0.4 rad). Participants with lower placement noise placed their nets with less variability within a latent state (observed within-state variability, median 24° against 40° in C1 and C2) and with smaller error relative to the hidden-state target (50° against 66°). The prior was bounded at 0.873 rad (50°), and for 11 participants (all in C1 and C2) the 95 % posterior interval reached this bound; these participants had the most variable placements (median within-state variability 45°, against 30° in the others), and their placement noise is therefore estimated with an upper limit.

Noise reactivity. Noise reactivity was lower in C3 (median 0.33) than in C1 and C2 (1.70 and 1.37), and 5 of the 8 posterior means within 5 % of the prior range from the lower bound were in C3. In the model, a low value means that a displaced outcome is rarely attributed to an oddball and is instead treated as evidence for a change of latent state. Participants in C3 had been told that the attack directions shift by about 120° at irregular intervals, but not that single displaced attacks occur. Noise reactivity is the least precisely estimated parameter (recovery slope 0.59; section 2.3.2), so that values in the centre of the prior are drawn toward it.

Precision weighting, belief momentum and switch probability. These three parameters were right-skewed (skewness 1.20, 1.26 and 0.97), without differences between the condition medians of a similar size as for the three parameters above. Precision weighting had three high values (3.6 to 4.9; two in C1), belief momentum had values above 0.5 for 12 participants (all in C1 and C2), and the posterior means of the switch probability lay within 5 % of the prior range from the lower bound for 6 participants.



Figure 11:Posterior means of the six parameters by instruction condition for all 68 participants. Filled points: participants assigned the latent-state model; open points: participants assigned another model. Thin vertical lines: central 95 % posterior intervals. Black bars: median and interquartile range of the posterior means. Dashed lines: bounds of the uniform prior.

Instruction effects on the parameters. In linear models of the posterior means (standardized) with the planned contrasts (59 participants assigned the latent-state model), participants told the structure (C3) had lower placement noise (planned contrast C3 versus C1 and C2 = −1.49 parameter SDs, SE = 0.248, t(56) = −6.02, p < .001, q < .001), lower noise reactivity (−1.22, SE = 0.275, t(56) = −4.43, p < .001, q < .001), higher cue sensitivity (1.14, SE = 0.279, t(56) = 4.09, p < .001, q < .001) and lower belief momentum (−0.64, SE = 0.306, t(56) = −2.08, p = .042, q = .063; HC3, p = .007) than participants not told it. Precision weighting (−0.23, p = .47) and the switch probability (−0.30, p = .35) did not differ, and no parameter differed between C2 and C1 (largest, precision weighting, −0.56, p = .060). Instruction therefore changed how precisely and how consistently the nets were placed relative to the predicted direction, how fully the cue offset was represented and how readily a displaced attack was taken as a change of state, but not the expected rate of state changes.

Instruction effects on behaviour and the parameters. When the six parameters were added to linear models of the participant-level RQ1 outcomes, the planned contrast between C3 and C1 and C2 decreased by 83 % for the error relative to the hidden-state target (from −1.62 to −0.28 SDs; with parameters, p = .12), by 89 % for the proportion of intercepted attacks (1.43 to 0.16, p = .40) and by 81 % for the shift after transitions relative to regular trials (1.34 to 0.26, p = .44), and condition no longer explained variance beyond the parameters (F-tests of condition given the parameters, p = .30, .70 and .60). For the proportion of split allocations, the contrast decreased by 36 % and remained significant (−0.88 to −0.56, p = .019). For the transfer of a transition to the second cue (|I_e|; −1.07 to −1.39, p < .001) and the additional weight on state error (1.97 to 1.42, p < .001), the instruction effect was not accounted for by the parameters (F-tests of condition given the parameters, p < .001 for both). The parameters thus describe the instruction effects on accuracy, interception and the response to transitions, but not those on the transfer of a change to the second cue and on the selective correction of state error.

hierarchy.lvl3: 2.3 Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores? (RQ3)
2.3 Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores? (RQ3)

records.content:
The associations of the five questionnaires with the six parameters were estimated with the participant-level linear models described in section 1.5.3, in an across-condition form and a moderation form, in all 65 participants with questionnaire data and in the 57 of them assigned the latent-state model (C1, 20; C2, 25; C3, 12). Of the 90 tests per sample (six parameters × five questionnaires × three terms: the questionnaire term of the across-condition model, and the questionnaire term and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation model), one remained significant after the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the five questionnaires.

Belief momentum and STICSA state anxiety. In the participants assigned the latent-state model, the across-condition model of belief momentum showed a significant questionnaire term for STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 53) = 7.45, p = .009, q = .043): higher state anxiety was associated with higher belief momentum (slope = 0.34 parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, 95 % CI [0.09, 0.59]; 0.076 units of belief momentum per SD). The association was retained with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (p = .015) and when the uncertainty of the individual estimates was included by pooling over posterior draws (slope = 0.33, SE = 0.163, t(38.1) = 2.05, p = .047; 24 % of the variance of the pooled coefficient was due to the uncertainty of the estimates). In the moderation form, the slope did not differ between conditions (condition × STICSA state F(2, 51) = 0.01, p = .99; slopes in C1, C2 and C3 = 0.38, 0.33 and 0.34). No single participant determined the association: when each participant was left out in turn, the across-condition slope remained between 0.28 and 0.42 (p = .001 to .029; largest Cook’s distance 0.17). In all 65 participants, the across-condition slope was smaller and did not survive the correction (0.26, 95 % CI [0.02, 0.50], F(1, 61) = 4.50, p = .038, q = .15).

Incremental validity of belief momentum. In a linear model of STICSA state anxiety (z) with condition and belief momentum, the standardized coefficient of belief momentum was 0.36 (p = .009; latent-state sample). When the three behavioural markers of belief momentum were added, it decreased to 0.24 (SE = 0.168, F(1, 50) = 2.00, p = .163; HC3, p = .217; change of R² = 0.032), whereas the markers together were associated with STICSA state anxiety (p = .039). Of the markers, the error on the first placement after an episode transition was correlated with both belief momentum (r = .45) and STICSA state anxiety (r = .36, p = .005); the change of the placement centre after transitions was correlated with belief momentum (r = −.52) but not significantly with STICSA state anxiety (r = −.20, p = .14). The association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety is therefore largely shared with the higher error on the first placement after a transition, the participant-level counterpart of the association of STICSA state anxiety in Model B1 (section 2.2.2), and the parameter does not carry information about STICSA state anxiety beyond these markers. In the model, this higher error corresponds to a belief about the active state that follows the evidence of the displaced attack more slowly. In the model, higher belief momentum means that the belief about the active latent state moves less toward the evidence of each new outcome, that is, that the belief is revised more slowly.

Further associations that did not survive the correction. In all 65 participants, the questionnaire term of the moderation model of belief momentum was significant for OCI before correction (F(1, 59) = 7.04, p = .010, q = .051), with the steepest slope in C3 (0.83 parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, 95 % CI [0.15, 1.52], against 0.21 in C1 and 0.12 in C2; condition × OCI F(2, 59) = 1.78, p = .18); in the participants assigned the latent-state model, this term was not significant (p = .25). Higher STICSA state anxiety was associated with lower precision weighting in both samples (across-condition slope = −0.23 and −0.24, p = .064 and .067); with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, this association was significant in all 65 participants (p = .009, q = .045) but not when the uncertainty of the estimates was included (p = .069). For the switch probability, the condition dependence of the OCI slope was significant before correction in all participants (condition × OCI F(2, 59) = 3.80, p = .028, q = .14), carried by the contrast between C2 and C1 (planned contrast of the slopes = −0.59, p = .038). For noise reactivity, cue sensitivity and placement noise, none of the three terms had p < .05 for any questionnaire in either sample.

The earlier analysis with partial correlations, in which each questionnaire was adjusted for the remaining scales, had shown a negative association between STICSA trait anxiety and the switch probability (partial r = −.34). In the models with one questionnaire at a time used here, this association was not present (across-condition slope, p = .17 in all participants and p = .52 in the participants assigned the latent-state model).



Figure 12:Questionnaire slopes of the six parameters from the across-condition models (parameter SDs per questionnaire SD), in all participants and in the participants assigned the latent-state model. Points are estimates and thick lines 95 % confidence intervals; filled points mark intervals that exclude zero (unadjusted). Thin lines are the 95 % intervals pooled over 100 posterior draws per participant.



Figure 13:Questionnaire slopes of the six parameters within each instruction condition, from the moderation models in all participants.

2.3 Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores? (RQ3)

records.content: Net placement behaviour was best described by the latent-state model for 59 of 68 participants, and by neither of the two models that track a single direction for any participant. The six parameters of the latent-state model were calibrated and recovered from simulated sessions with correlations of .79 to .998, and the fitted model reproduced the differences between participants in the levels of the behaviours from which the parameters are estimated. Five of the six parameters correlated with the behavioural measure that follows from their definition. Of the associations between questionnaire scores and parameters, one survived the correction for the five questionnaires: higher STICSA state anxiety with higher belief momentum, in the participants assigned the latent-state model.

The diagnostics of all models are reported in 

Model Diagnostics, where the models carry the identifiers of the analysis scripts (given in parentheses below). For the models as reported here, the assumptions were met without relevant departures for the error relative to the hidden-state target (M1, M1, and A1; skewness of the standardized conditional residuals −0.31, excess kurtosis −0.10, 0.1 % beyond ±3; ratio of the residual SDs between conditions 1.05), for the binomial models of interception (M5, M7, and A2) and of a split allocation (M2, M3; quantile residuals consistent with uniformity, Kolmogorov–Smirnov p = .52 to .84, dispersion ratio 1.00 to 1.02), and for the change of the placement centre (M3, M4a; skewness −0.54, excess kurtosis −0.16, 0.1 % beyond ±3).

The diagnostics changed three models. (i) In M3, 4.4 % of trials without any change of the placement centre (C1, 3.9 %; C2, 3.4 %; C3, 7.6 %) had formed a separate cluster about four residual SDs below the other trials under log(shift + 0.001) (skewness −2.35, excess kurtosis 6.80, 4.1 % beyond ±3, singular fit); with log(shift + 1) this cluster disappeared and the fit was no longer singular. (ii) The circular variance of the net positions, the former outcome of M2, was bimodal (stacked versus split allocations); neither the beta model of the circular variance (quantile residuals not uniform, Kolmogorov–Smirnov p < .001; dispersion ratio 1.15, p = .008) nor Gaussian models of the circular variance or the circular SD (excess kurtosis up to 38) described it, whereas the binomial model of a split allocation did. (iii) M7 and Model C reported convergence warnings with angles in degrees, which disappeared with angles in units of 10°. In Model C, whose primary model contains a random intercept only, the questionnaire terms were not significant with cluster-robust standard errors (section 2.2.4).

The remaining departures were addressed by repeating every test of the linear mixed models with cluster-robust standard errors. They concerned heavy-tailed residuals in B2 (excess kurtosis 3.7 to 3.8; 0.7 % beyond ±3) and, more moderately, in M7 and Model C (excess kurtosis about 2.0); residual variance that decreased with the fitted value for B1 (Spearman ρ = −.30), the cross-cue transfer (M4, M5, and D; ρ = −.21 to −.24) and the error profile after transitions (M6, profile_transition; ρ = −.40); and non-normal participant random intercepts in M4 and D (Shapiro–Wilk p = .001 to .012). The planned contrasts of the RQ1 models were unchanged in their conclusions with cluster-robust standard errors except for the condition dependence of the shift after oddballs in M3 (section 2.1.2). The prediction error and the state error remain correlated by construction (variance inflation factor of the state error about 7), so that the two weights are estimated with correspondingly larger standard errors.

Participant-level models of the parameters (RQ3). The residuals were not normally distributed in 109 of the 120 models (Shapiro–Wilk p < .05), mostly because of the skewed and bimodal distributions of the parameters (section 2.3.5), and the Breusch–Pagan test indicated heteroscedasticity in 34 models (cue sensitivity, 20; noise reactivity, 11), which is why all tested terms were also tested with HC3 standard errors. For the association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety in the participants assigned the latent-state model, no participant had a large influence (largest Cook’s distance 0.17), and the across-condition slope remained between 0.28 and 0.42 (p = .001 to .029) when each participant was left out in turn. The largest Cook’s distance of any model was 1.03 (noise reactivity, BDI, latent-state sample).

The three research questions meet in the response to a single displaced attack. Instruction about the structure (RQ1) lowered the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, increased the proportion of intercepted mosquito attacks, reduced the proportion of trials with splitted net allocation centers (WE NEED A BETTER WORDING FOR THE NET PLACEMENT SPLIT BUT IDK YET), increased the change of the placement after episode transitions relative to oddballs, increased the transfer of an episode transition to the second color cue and increased the selective correction of state error relative to outcome noise; the planned contrast between C2 and C1 was not significant for any of these outcomes. Higher STICSA state and trait anxiety and OCI scores were associated with a higher net plaxement error on the first net placement after an episode transition, but not after an oddball, and with a wider allocation after oddballs than after episode transitions on the first net placement after the event (RQ2, Models B1 and B2; retained with cluster-robust standard errors). At the level of the computational model (RQ3), the latent-state model described the behaviour of 59 of 68 participants, and higher STICSA state anxiety was associated with higher belief momentum; this association was largely shared with the higher error on the first placement after a transition, so that the parameter describes the behavioural association of Model B1 as a slower revision of the belief about the active state, thereby providing one possible mechanism of belief updating giving rise to the observed behavioral tendencies. The parameters described the instruction effects on accuracy, interception and the response to episode transitions, but not those on the transfer to the second cue (because the current inference agent shares the latent state across cues, so it has no individual dimension for transfer --> TO BE DISICUSSED IF WE WANT TO TRY TO ADD A SEVENTH PARAMETER BUT PROBABLY ONLY WEAKLY IDENTIFIABLE) and the selective correction of state error (BECAUSE IT IS NO SIMPLE LR MODEL).

(INTERPRETATION AND DISCUSSION: see the draft in results/archiv/discussion_draft_until_2026-10-13.md; its quantitative statements partially refer to analyses that are no longer part of the analysis set and have to be replaced by the results above)

Analyses

questionnaire × parameter models with HC3, plausible values and leave-one-out; incremental validity (tambi_rq3_models.R, tambi_parameter_validation.R)

Assumptions of all models

tambi_model_diagnostics.R (

Model Diagnostics)

Open analyses (front page): the model comparison with placement noise in all models, the split-half reliability, the power analysis by simulation, and the in-task affect models with the coding of the RQ2 models.

All mixed models are fitted with lme4/lmerTest (REML, bobyqa, Satterthwaite df) or glmmTMB (binomial), with instruction condition as an unordered factor with the sum-to-zero planned contrasts C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3) and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0). The three instruction conditions are the primary between-subjects manipulation in TAMBI. They vary in how much explicit structural information participants receive about the cue–direction relationships and episode transitions before the task begins.
This manipulation doesn’t just allow the comparison of learning-from-scratch with partial and complete structural knowledge, but also creates a between-condition manipulation of structural priors, representing exposure to different levels of task ambiguity.

Instruction condition is randomly assigned to each participant before the session and determines which set of instruction slides is presented by the PsychoPy script.
Three instruction conditions with different levels of Task Ambiguity, corresponding to different levels of epistemic (teal) and aleatoric (purple) uncertainty.

The visual layout of the task (circular “arena”, 32 slots)

How to place nets (left click) and remove them (right click)

That mosquitoes will attack, and that placing nets in the attack direction will block them with a certain probability depending on the number of nets, stacked in the respective slot.

That a systematic angular offset exists between the two cues

That the direction pattern can change over the course of the experiment

That oddballs exist

Corresponding computational models: Condition 2 corresponds approximately to models that know a structure exists but must infer its parameters - most closely M3 (full Bayesian inference) and the temporal commitment models M_sticky, M_count, and M_hybrid.

Participants learn everything in Condition 2, plus:

Rule 3 (Cue Offset): The instructions explain that one color consistently predicts attacks from one angular region, while the other color consistently predicts attacks offset by approximately 70° clockwise from the first. An example illustration shows the direction pattern for both colors.

Rule 2 (Episode Rotation): The instructions explain that at irregular intervals (approximately every 20 trials), the entire direction pattern shifts by approximately 120°. Both cues shift simultaneously. The transition is not announced.

The instruction slides for Condition 3 are direction-dependent: the example illustration showing the cue–direction relationship is adapted to match the actual direction pattern in the participant’s trial schedule. This requires knowing the first occurrence of each color cue in the schedule and the corresponding attack direction, which is pre-computed from the schedule file before the session starts.

Instruction conditions are assigned randomly with automatic balancing across conditions.

Randomization is implemented at the schedule level as well as at the condition level: participants are assigned to condition before the session begins, and the assignment is documented in the results file. Trial schedules are drawn randomly from the pre-generated pool before presenting the condition-specific (and for condition 3 also trial-schedule-specific) instruction slides.

All participants complete the same practice trial regardless of condition. The practice is a free-exploration phase with progressive hints:

If no net has been placed yet: “Try left-clicking on one of the white circles to place a net”

If one net has been placed but not multiple: “Good! Try placing more nets in different positions”

If multiple nets placed but none removed: “Now try right-clicking on a net to remove it”

When at least one net has been placed and one removed: “Perfect! [Space to continue]”

The practice arena shows the standard display but without any cue color (no actual trial is run). The participant’s placement behavior is recorded but not scored. The practice trial ends when the participant presses Space after having both placed and removed at least one net.

At the end of the session, all participants complete a questionnaire that includes a rule awareness check:

Page C (Yes/No): “Did you notice that the direction of the mosquitoes changed in a consistent way depending on the color cue that was shown?”

Page D (text input, if Yes): “How did the direction of the mosquito change depending on which color cue was shown?”

Page E (Yes/No): “Were the instructions at the beginning of the experiment clear and comprehensible?”

Page F (text input, if No): “What specifically was unclear?”

These items allow post-hoc verification of rule awareness across conditions and identification of any participants in Conditions 1 or 2 who spontaneously discovered the structural rules, or any participants in Condition 3 who failed to encode the instructions.

The screen coordinate system uses degrees of visual angle with the origin at the center of the screen. All slot positions are computed analytically from the angle formula:def angle_to_position(self, angle_deg, radius=8):
    angle_rad = math.radians(angle_deg)
    x = radius * math.cos(angle_rad)
    y = radius * math.sin(angle_rad)
    return [x, y]

The 32 slots are positioned at equal angular intervals (11.25° per slot) on the defense perimeter circle. Slot 0 is at 0° (3 o’clock position in standard math coordinates). The slot assignment for a mouse click uses nearest-slot logic:def get_slot_from_position(self, pos):
    min_distance = float('inf')
    closest_slot = None
    for i, slot_pos in enumerate(self.slot_positions):
        distance = math.sqrt((pos[0]-slot_pos[0])**2 + (pos[1]-slot_pos[1])**2)
        if distance < min_distance:
            min_distance = distance
            closest_slot = i
    return closest_slot if min_distance < 1.5 else None

The 1.5° threshold means that clicks far from all slots (e.g., near the center or outside the circle) are not registered.

Net orientation at each slot is tangential to the perimeter circle:net.ori = 90 - angle  # Rotate net to be tangent to circle

The Mosquito Defense Task is a spatial predictive inference paradigm implemented in PsychoPy. On each trial, participants allocate up to 7 defensive nets across 32 evenly spaced angular positions on a circular perimeter, with the goal of intercepting a mosquito that will subsequently attack from a direction governed by the task’s latent structure.

The task is presented with a narrative and visual framing (described in 

Gamification and Game Design) in which the participant is a defender protecting a central resource from mosquito attacks. The spatial, circular structure of the defense problem directly embodies the angular inference problem that is the scientific focus of the study.

The central visual display consists of:

A central light cue circle that changes color each trial to indicate the active cue identity. During the anticipation phase, this cue is visible; during barrier placement, it remains visible.

A defense perimeter circle on which the 32 slots are positioned at equal angular intervals (11.25° per slot).

32 slot indicators - small white circles at each slot position indicating available placement positions.

A blood counter arc - a colored arc on an inner circle indicating the current blood point total (initially 100, updated after each outcome trial).

Net visuals - image-based net stimuli that appear at slot positions when barriers are placed.

Mouse cursor - a small red circle showing the current cursor position, accompanied by a small net image and a counter showing remaining nets.

The color cue appears at the center of the screen. No net placement is permitted during this phase. The cursor is centered at the start of each trial.

Purpose: The anticipation phase gives participants time to form their prediction about the attack direction and plan their net placement, without allowing pre-commitment.

Duration: Fixed at 4.0 seconds.

Eye tracking marker: ANTICIPATION_START / ANTICIPATION_END

BIOPAC marker: ANTICIPATION_START_EP{episode}

Participants use the mouse to place nets on the perimeter slots. The mouse cursor is visible and interactive during this phase.

Left click: Place one net at the nearest slot to the cursor position.

Right click: Remove one net from the slot nearest the cursor (if the slot contains at least one net).

Maximum nets: 7 per trial. Participants may place fewer; they do not need to use all 7.

Stacking: Multiple nets may be placed in the same slot, up to 7. The defense effectiveness of stacked nets follows a cubic decline function (see 

Outcomes).

Time limit: 7.0 seconds. Visual countdown is not displayed, but audio beeps sound at 3s, 2s, and 1s remaining.

Early advancement: The phase ends early if all 7 nets are placed (though participants may continue repositioning until time expires or they press no further keys).

The cursor display during placement shows: a small net image offset from the cursor, a counter displaying remaining nets (e.g., 5/7), and a hover highlight on the nearest slot.

Slot assignment uses nearest-slot logic: the clicked position maps to whichever of the 32 slots is closest. Slots are positioned at radius 8° from center; clicks anywhere on the screen are mapped to the nearest slot.

Eye tracking marker: PLACEMENT_START / PLACEMENT_END

A jittered delay between net placement and outcome delivery. The color cue remains visible. No new interactions are possible.

Duration: Drawn from a truncated exponential distribution: \text{ISI} \sim \min(\text{Exp}(\lambda = 0.5) + 2.0, 4.0) seconds.

Purpose: Prevents participants from anticipating outcome onset from a fixed delay; adds temporal jitter for physiological data analysis.

Eye tracking marker: ISI_START / ISI_END
The outcome phase varies depending on whether the current trial is an outcome trial or an omission trial.

The mosquito approaches from the attack angle, animated over 2.3 seconds. The mosquito image is selected based on the attack direction (8 directional variants: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW). The mosquito buzz sound plays throughout the animation.

Blocked outcome: If the mosquito encounters a net in its approach slot, it reverses and flies back. The show_blood_gain_feedback() function displays a green sparkle animation, “+1 ♥” rising animation, and “BLOCKED!” text. Blood points increase by 1.

Hit outcome: The mosquito reaches the center. The show_blood_loss_feedback() function displays a red flash overlay, screen shake effect, “-1 ♥” falling animation, and “BITE!” text. Blood points decrease by 1.

Participants begin with 100 blood points. Points change by ±1 per outcome trial (no change on omission trials). The blood counter is displayed continuously as:

A numerical value at center screen

A colored arc on the inner circle that shrinks as blood points decrease

A heart symbol (♥) whose color shifts from green (>60 points) to yellow-orange (30–60) to red (<30 points)

The blood counter has no mechanical consequence in the current implementation — it does not end the experiment and does not trigger any qualitative state change. It functions purely as a continuous feedback display of cumulative performance, providing motivational salience to individual trial outcomes.

Scheduled breaks occur approximately every 40–60 trials (randomized to avoid episode boundary overlap). The break screen is displayed until the participant presses Space, after which an experimenter confirmation screen waits for the experimenter to press ‘P’ before the experiment resumes. Maximum break duration is 3 minutes. After each break, a drift correction is performed and a 3-2-1 countdown is shown before the next trial begins.

Within-task emotional state ratings are collected 1–2 times per episode. The rating is triggered at either trial 7 or trial 14 of the episode (randomly chosen per episode), but not both. If not triggered at trial 7 (50% chance), it is triggered at trial 14 by default.

The rating screen presents six continuous sliders (valence, arousal, anxiety, stress, frustration, fatigue) in randomized order. Participants drag the sliders with the mouse. The rating is confirmed by pressing Space.

Trial schedules are pre-generated as CSV files and stored in the trial_schedules/ directory. One schedule file is selected randomly at session start, ensuring that trial properties are rigorously controlled while still providing participant-level randomization. This approach avoids the risk of generating invalid schedules at runtime (e.g., constraint violations) and enables efficient session startup, ensuring low susceptibility to errors.

Each schedule file is generated by the trial_schedule_generation.ipynb notebook and encodes all trial-level information needed by the PsychoPy task: episode membership, cue color, target angle, observed angle (target + von Mises noise), outcome occurrence, and oddball flag.

Episode lengths are drawn to satisfy:

Each length is in the range [16, 24] trials

The mean across all 9 episodes is in [19, 21] trials

The generation procedure iteratively adjusts lengths until both constraints are satisfied. The jitter ensures that participants cannot use trial counting to predict episode transitions.

The boundary constraint is the most demanding structural requirement: the last trial of each episode and the first trial of the next episode must display the same color cue. This prevents a cue switch from co-occurring with an episode transition, ensuring that the only signal of a transition is the change in attack direction.

A secondary constraint requires that:

Episodes 2–5 each begin with 3–4 consecutive trials of the cue that initiates the learning phase

The learning-phase cue identities are balanced (2 of each identity in episodes 2–5)

All 8 episode transition cues are balanced (4 of each identity)

The planning algorithm proceeds as follows:

Generate a balanced sequence of transition cue identities (4 of identity 1, 4 of identity 2, with the first 4 balanced 2:2).

For each episode, attempt to generate a valid cue sequence satisfying:

Required start color (= last color of previous episode, if available)

Required learning-phase start color (for episodes 2–5)

Maximum within-episode color streak of 3

Approximately equal representation of both colors within the episode

If any episode produces a conflict between the boundary constraint and the learning-phase identity requirement, discard the current identity sequence and retry with a new one.

This procedure is iterated up to 1000 times. In practice, a valid plan is almost always found within ~50 attempts.

After the cue sequence is determined, outcome omission trials are assigned per episode:

Valid positions for omissions exclude:

The first 4 trials of each episode (learning phase)

The last trial of each episode

Trials immediately following a cue switch

Placement algorithm:

Compute target omission count based on a random rate drawn from [5%, 15%]

Select omission positions from valid positions, avoiding consecutive omissions where possible

If strict non-consecutive selection cannot achieve the target count, allow consecutive omissions

Oddballs are assigned after omissions, with additional constraints:

Valid positions for oddballs additionally exclude:

Trials that are already omission trials

Trials immediately adjacent (±1) to omission trials

Consecutive oddball avoidance: If the target count cannot be achieved without consecutive oddballs, the target is reduced rather than allowing consecutive oddballs.

Overlap check: A validation step confirms that no trial is simultaneously an omission and an oddball. The schedule generation notebook reports the overlap count, which must be 0.

For each trial:

The target angle is computed from:

The current episode’s base angle (= initial_start_angle for odd episodes, initial_start_angle + 120° for even episodes)

The cue identity (identity 2 adds rule3_shift = 70° to the base angle)

The actual angle is obtained by adding von Mises noise:\omega_t \sim \mathcal{VM}(\mu_{\text{target}},\, \kappa = 40)

This gives a typical angular deviation of approximately ±10° (SD ≈ 10°, range ≈ 50°, maximum range is constrained to < 60°), matching the concentration parameter used in the simulation models.

For oddball trials, the target angle is first shifted by +120°, then the same noise process is applied.

#============================================================#

# function to add angle noise 
# Args:
#   - target_angle in degree
#   - noise_std in degree
#   - use_gaussian: True for gaussian noise, false for von Mises based noise
# Returns:
#   - angle with noise in degree (0-360) --> Stimulus angle

def add_angle_noise(target_angle, kappa_noise=kappa, use_gaussian=False):
        
    # Sample from von Mises distribution centred around target_angle
    target_rad = np.radians(target_angle)
    noisy_rad = vonmises.rvs(kappa_noise, loc=target_rad)
    noisy_angle = np.degrees(noisy_rad) % 360
    
    return noisy_angle

def generate_balanced_episode_lengths(n_episodes, base_length, min_length, max_length, target_mean_min, target_mean_max):
   
    target_total = base_length * n_episodes  # Target total trials
    
    while True:
        # Generate random lengths within the allowed range
        lengths = []
        for i in range(n_episodes):
            length = random.randint(min_length, max_length)
            lengths.append(length)
        
        # Check if the mean is within acceptable range
        actual_mean = sum(lengths) / n_episodes
        
        if target_mean_min <= actual_mean <= target_mean_max:
            return lengths
        
        # If mean is too low or too high, adjust some episodes
        if actual_mean < target_mean_min:
            # Need to increase some episodes
            deficit = target_total - sum(lengths)
            for i in range(min(deficit, n_episodes)):
                if lengths[i] < max_length:
                    lengths[i] += 1
        elif actual_mean > target_mean_max:
            # Need to decrease some episodes  
            excess = sum(lengths) - target_total
            for i in range(min(excess, n_episodes)):
                if lengths[i] > min_length:
                    lengths[i] -= 1
        
        # Check again
        actual_mean = sum(lengths) / n_episodes
        if target_mean_min <= actual_mean <= target_mean_max:
            return lengths

def assign_outcomes_per_episode(trials, min_rate=min_omission_rate, max_rate=max_omission_rate, target_overall=target_overall_omission_rate):
    
    outcomes = np.ones(len(trials))
    
    # Group trials by episode
    episodes = {}
    for i, trial in enumerate(trials):
        ep = trial['episode']
        if ep not in episodes:
            episodes[ep] = []
        episodes[ep].append(i)

    episode_rates = {}
    total_omissions_assigned = 0

    # Schritt 1: Für jede Episode exakte Anzahl basierend auf Episode-Rate bestimmen
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        
        # Zufällige Rate innerhalb der erlaubten Grenzen
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_omissions = round(episode_length * episode_rate)
        
        # Strikt innerhalb min/max bounds halten
        min_allowed = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_allowed = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_omissions = max(min_allowed, min(max_allowed, target_omissions))

        # Valide Positionen bestimmen
        valid_indices = []
        for i in trial_indices:
            trial = trials[i]
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] <= 4:   # learning phase
                continue
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] == trial['episode_length']:  # last trial
                continue
            if i > 0 and trials[i]['cue_color'] != trials[i-1]['cue_color']:  # cue switch
                continue
            valid_indices.append(i)

        # Anzahl an verfügbare Positionen anpassen falls nötig
        if len(valid_indices) < target_omissions:
            print(f"[Warnung] Episode {episode_num}: nur {len(valid_indices)} gültige Positionen "
                  f"für {target_omissions} gewünschte Omissions")
            target_omissions = len(valid_indices)

        # Deterministische Auswahl ohne consecutive
        random.shuffle(valid_indices)
        selected = []
        for candidate in valid_indices:
            if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected):
                selected.append(candidate)
            if len(selected) >= target_omissions:
                break

        # Falls nicht genug non-consecutive Positionen verfügbar, fülle mit beliebigen auf
        if len(selected) < target_omissions:
            remaining_valid = [idx for idx in valid_indices if idx not in selected]
            needed = target_omissions - len(selected)
            random.shuffle(remaining_valid)
            selected.extend(remaining_valid[:needed])

        # Omissions setzen
        for idx in selected:
            outcomes[idx] = 0

        total_omissions_assigned += len(selected)
        actual_rate = len(selected) / episode_length if episode_length > 0 else 0
        episode_rates[episode_num] = actual_rate

        print(f"Episode {episode_num}: Ziel={target_omissions}, "
              f"gesetzt={len(selected)}, "
              f"Rate={actual_rate:.2%} (min={min_rate:.2%}, max={max_rate:.2%})")

    # Finale Statistiken
    overall_rate = total_omissions_assigned / len(trials)
    print(f"\n[Final] Gesamt: {total_omissions_assigned}/{len(trials)} "
          f"= {overall_rate:.2%}, Ziel={target_overall:.2%}")

    return outcomes, episode_rates, overall_rate

def assign_oddballs_per_episode(trials, outcomes, min_rate=min_oddball_rate, max_rate=max_oddball_rate, target_overall=oddball_rate):
    
    oddballs = np.zeros(len(trials))
    
    # Group trials by episode
    episodes = {}
    for i, trial in enumerate(trials):
        ep = trial['episode']
        if ep not in episodes:
            episodes[ep] = []
        episodes[ep].append(i)

    episode_targets = {}
    episode_assigned = {}
    episode_rates = {}
    episode_valid_indices = {}
    total_oddballs_assigned = 0

    # Schritt 1: pro Episode grobe Rate bestimmen
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_oddballs = round(episode_length * episode_rate)

        # min/max bounds
        min_possible = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_possible = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_oddballs = max(min_possible, min(max_possible, target_oddballs))

        episode_targets[episode_num] = target_oddballs

    # Schritt 2: oddballs tatsächlich zuweisen (ohne globales Balancing)
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        
        # Zufällige Rate innerhalb der erlaubten Grenzen
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_oddballs = round(episode_length * episode_rate)
        
        # Strikt innerhalb min/max bounds halten
        min_allowed = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_allowed = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_oddballs = max(min_allowed, min(max_allowed, target_oddballs))

        # valide Positionen bestimmen (gleiche Restriktionen wie outcomes + keine outcome omissions + nicht vor outcome omissions)
        valid_indices = []
        for i in trial_indices:
            trial = trials[i]
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] <= 4:   # learning phase
                continue
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] == trial['episode_length']:  # letztes Trial
                continue
            if i > 0 and trials[i]['cue_color'] != trials[i-1]['cue_color']:  # cue switch
                continue
            if outcomes[i] == 0:  # bereits outcome omission
                continue
            if i+1 < len(outcomes) and outcomes[i+1] == 0:  # nächstes Trial ist outcome omission
                continue
            if i-1 >= 0 and outcomes[i-1] == 0:  # vorheriges Trial ist outcome omission
                continue
            valid_indices.append(i)

        if len(valid_indices) < target_oddballs:
            print(f"[Warnung] Episode {episode_num}: nur {len(valid_indices)} gültige Positionen "
                  f"für {target_oddballs} gewünschte Oddballs")
            target_oddballs = len(valid_indices)

        # deterministische Auswahl ohne consecutive
        random.shuffle(valid_indices)
        selected = []
        for candidate in valid_indices:
            if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected):
                selected.append(candidate)
            if len(selected) >= target_oddballs:
                break

        # Falls nicht genug non-consecutive Positionen verfügbar, versuche weniger strikt
        if len(selected) < target_oddballs:
            remaining_valid = [idx for idx in valid_indices if idx not in selected]
            needed = target_oddballs - len(selected)
            
            # Versuche erst noch non-consecutive zu finden
            for candidate in remaining_valid:
                if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected) and len(selected) < target_oddballs:
                    selected.append(candidate)
            
            # Falls immer noch nicht genug, reduziere das Ziel anstatt consecutive zu erlauben
            if len(selected) < target_oddballs:
                print(f"[Info] Episode {episode_num}: Reduziere Oddball-Ziel von {target_oddballs} auf {len(selected)} "
                      f"um consecutive Oddballs zu vermeiden")
                target_oddballs = len(selected)

        for idx in selected:
            oddballs[idx] = 1

        total_oddballs_assigned += len(selected)
        episode_assigned[episode_num] = len(selected)
        actual_rate = len(selected) / episode_length if episode_length > 0 else 0
        episode_rates[episode_num] = actual_rate

        print(f"Episode {episode_num}: Oddball Ziel={target_oddballs}, "
              f"gesetzt={len(selected)}, "
              f"Rate={actual_rate:.2%} (min={min_rate:.2%}, max={max_rate:.2%})")

    # Finale Statistiken ohne globales Balancing
    total_oddballs = int(np.sum(oddballs))
    overall_rate = total_oddballs / len(trials)

    print(f"\n[Final Oddball] Gesamt: {total_oddballs}/{len(trials)} "
          f"= {overall_rate:.2%}, Ziel={target_overall:.2%}")

    return oddballs, episode_rates, overall_rate

def generate_valid_cue_sequence(n_trials, required_start_color=None, required_end_color=None, episode_num=1, learning_phase_trials=0):
    
    for attempt in range(max_sequence_attempts):
        # Calculate number of trials per color (approximately half each -> 10 +/- 2 on average)
        n_color1 = random.randint(max(1, n_trials//2 - 2), min(n_trials-1, n_trials//2 + 2))
        n_color2 = n_trials - n_color1
        
        counts = {cue_colors[0]: 0, cue_colors[1]: 0}
        sequence = []
        
        # Handle learning phase trials at the start
        learning_trials_added = 0
        if learning_phase_trials > 0 and required_start_color:
            for i in range(min(learning_phase_trials, n_trials)):
                sequence.append(required_start_color)
                counts[required_start_color] += 1
                learning_trials_added += 1
        
        # Fill remaining positions
        remaining_positions = n_trials - learning_trials_added
        if required_end_color and remaining_positions > 0:
            remaining_positions -= 1  
        
        # Calculate remaining quota for each color
        remaining_color1 = n_color1 - counts[cue_colors[0]]
        remaining_color2 = n_color2 - counts[cue_colors[1]]
        
        # Adjust if end color requirement affects quota
        if required_end_color:
            if required_end_color == cue_colors[0]:
                remaining_color1 -= 1
            else:
                remaining_color2 -= 1
        
        # Generate middle section randomly while respecting quotas and streak limits
        temp_counts = {cue_colors[0]: remaining_color1, cue_colors[1]: remaining_color2}
        
        for pos in range(remaining_positions):
            available_colors = [c for c in cue_colors if temp_counts[c] > 0]
            
            # Enforce max streak constraint
            if len(sequence) >= max_same_color_streak:
                if all(color == sequence[-1] for color in sequence[-max_same_color_streak:]):
                    if sequence[-1] in available_colors:
                        available_colors.remove(sequence[-1])
            
            if not available_colors:
                break  # Failed this attempt, try again
            
            chosen_color = random.choice(available_colors)
            sequence.append(chosen_color)
            temp_counts[chosen_color] -= 1
        
        # Add required end color if specified
        if required_end_color and len(sequence) == n_trials - 1:
            sequence.append(required_end_color)
            counts[required_end_color] += 1
        
        # Verify the sequence meets all requirements
        if (len(sequence) == n_trials and 
            sequence.count(cue_colors[0]) == n_color1 and 
            sequence.count(cue_colors[1]) == n_color2 and
            (not required_start_color or sequence[0] == required_start_color) and
            (not required_end_color or sequence[-1] == required_end_color)):
            return sequence
    
    raise Exception(f"Could not generate valid sequence for episode {episode_num} after {max_sequence_attempts} attempts")

    oddball_rate
)

# Apply oddball modifications to actual_vector_angle and recalculate encodings
for i, is_oddball in enumerate(oddballs):
    if is_oddball:
        all_trials[i]['is_oddball'] = True
        
        # Apply 180° shift with noise to the original target angle
        oddball_target = (all_trials[i]['target_vector_angle'] + oddball_angle_shift) % 360
        oddball_actual = add_angle_noise(
            oddball_target,
            # noise_std=angle_noise_std,
            use_gaussian=use_gaussian_noise
        )
        
        # Update the trial data
        all_trials[i]['actual_vector_angle'] = round(oddball_actual, 2)
        
        # Recalculate angle noise
        angle_diff = (oddball_actual - oddball_target + 180) % 360 - 180
        all_trials[i]['angle_noise'] = angle_diff
        
    else:
        all_trials[i]['is_oddball'] = False

#=========================================================================#
# Convert to DataFrame
#=========================================================================#

df_trials = pd.DataFrame(all_trials)

# safe episode rates and overall rate in the df
for ep, rate in episode_rates.items():
    df_trials.loc[df_trials['episode'] == ep, 'omission_rate'] = rate

df_trials['overall_omission_rate'] = overall_rate

# safe oddball rates in the df
for ep, rate in oddball_episode_rates.items():
    df_trials.loc[df_trials['episode'] == ep, 'oddball_rate'] = rate

df_trials['overall_oddball_rate'] = overall_oddball_rate

#=========================================================================#
# Further checks / verifications
#=========================================================================#

# Show von Mises encoding parameters
print(f"\nVon Mises encoding parameters:")
print(f"Feature length: {feature_len} (resolution: {step_size:.1f}°)")
print(f"Kappa (concentration): {kappa}")

# Show example vector encoding for first few trials with noise information
print(f"\nExample vector encodings with noise (first 5 trials):")
for i in range(min(5, len(all_trials))):
    target_angle = all_trials[i]['target_vector_angle']
    actual_angle = all_trials[i]['actual_vector_angle']
    noise = all_trials[i]['angle_noise']
    if noise > 180:
        noise = noise - 360

# Analyze noise statistics
angle_noises = []
for trial in all_trials:
    noise = trial['angle_noise']
    if noise > 180:  
        noise = noise - 360
    angle_noises.append(noise)

angle_noises = np.array(angle_noises)
print(f"\nNoise statistics:")
print(f"Mean: {np.mean(angle_noises):.2f}°")
print(f"Std: {np.std(angle_noises):.2f}°")
print(f"Min: {np.min(angle_noises):.2f}°")
print(f"Max: {np.max(angle_noises):.2f}°")

# Show episode lengths to verify jitter
print("\nEpisode lengths:")
episode_lengths_check = df_trials.groupby('episode')['episode_length'].first()
for ep, length in episode_lengths_check.items():
    print(f"Episode {ep}: {length} trials")

# Show learning phase analysis for episodes 2-5
print("\nLearning phase analysis (Episodes 2-5):")
identity_count_2_5 = {1: 0, 2: 0}
for ep in range(2, min(n_episodes + 1, 6)):
    ep_data = df_trials[df_trials['episode'] == ep]
    if len(ep_data) > 0:
        first_4_cues = ep_data.head(4)['cue_identity'].tolist()
        start_identity = first_4_cues[0]
        identity_count_2_5[start_identity] += 1
        same_cue_count = 1
        for i in range(1, len(first_4_cues)):
            if first_4_cues[i] == first_4_cues[0]:
                same_cue_count += 1
            else:
                break
        print(f"Episode {ep}: {same_cue_count} consecutive trials with cue_identity {start_identity}")

print(f"Balance check (Episodes 2-5): Identity 1: {identity_count_2_5[1]}, Identity 2: {identity_count_2_5[2]}")

# Show balance for all 8 episode transitions
print("\nAll episode transitions balance (Episodes 2-9):")
identity_count_all = {1: 0, 2: 0}
for ep in range(2, min(n_episodes + 1, 10)):
    ep_data = df_trials[df_trials['episode'] == ep]
    if len(ep_data) > 0:
        start_identity = ep_data.head(1)['cue_identity'].iloc[0]
        identity_count_all[start_identity] += 1

print(f"Balance check (All transitions): Identity 1: {identity_count_all[1]}, Identity 2: {identity_count_all[2]}")

# Show boundary constraint
print("\nBoundary constraint -> same cue_identity before and after episode transition:")
for ep in range(2, min(n_episodes + 1, 10)):
    if ep > 1:
        prev_ep_data = df_trials[df_trials['episode'] == ep-1]
        curr_ep_data = df_trials[df_trials['episode'] == ep]
        if len(prev_ep_data) > 0 and len(curr_ep_data) > 0:
            last_cue_prev = prev_ep_data.tail(1)['cue_color'].iloc[0]
            first_cue_curr = curr_ep_data.head(1)['cue_color'].iloc[0]
            print(f"Episode {ep-1} → {ep}: {last_cue_prev} → {first_cue_curr} ({'✓' if last_cue_prev == first_cue_curr else '✗'})")

# Show omission rates
print("\nOmission rates:")
for ep in range(1, n_episodes + 1):
    ep_data = df_trials[df_trials['episode'] == ep]
    omissions = len(ep_data[ep_data['outcome_occurred'] == 0])
    total_trials = len(ep_data)
    rate = omissions / total_trials if total_trials > 0 else 0
    print(f"Episode {ep}: {omissions}/{total_trials} omissions ({rate:.1%})")

# Overall omission rate
total_omissions = len(df_trials[df_trials['outcome_occurred'] == 0])
total_trials = len(df_trials)
overall_rate = total_omissions / total_trials
print(f"Overall: {total_omissions}/{total_trials} omissions ({overall_rate:.1%})")
print(f"Target rate: {feedback_omission_rate:.1%}")

# Show oddball rates
print("\nOddball rates:")
for ep in range(1, n_episodes + 1):
    ep_data = df_trials[df_trials['episode'] == ep]
    oddballs = len(ep_data[ep_data['is_oddball'] == True])
    total_trials = len(ep_data)
    rate = oddballs / total_trials if total_trials > 0 else 0
    print(f"Episode {ep}: {oddballs}/{total_trials} oddballs ({rate:.1%})")

# Overall oddball rate
total_oddballs = len(df_trials[df_trials['is_oddball'] == True])
total_trials = len(df_trials)
overall_oddball_rate_check = total_oddballs / total_trials
print(f"Overall: {total_oddballs}/{total_trials} oddballs ({overall_oddball_rate_check:.1%})")
print(f"Target rate: {oddball_rate:.1%}")

# Check overlap between omissions and oddballs
overlap = len(df_trials[(df_trials['outcome_occurred'] == 0) & (df_trials['is_oddball'] == True)])
print(f"Overlap between omissions and oddballs: {overlap} (should be 0)")

# Show trial schedule preview
print(f"\nFirst 30 trials:")
print(df_trials.head(30)[['episode', 'trial_in_episode', 'cue_color', 'cue_identity', 'target_vector_angle', 'actual_vector_angle', 'outcome_occurred', 'is_oddball', 'trial_index']])

This guide will walk through building a MyST site, scrubbing source files, encrypting the HTML with a password, and deploying it to a separate public GitHub Pages repository - all automated via GitHub Actions.

You will need two repositories:

The Source Repo (private): contains your .md files, figures and/or other assets, myst.yml, toc.yml and optinally additional scripts to control the design etc.. (e.g. the repo your-username/study_documentation)

The Public Website Repo: will only contain the encrypted HTML output. (e.g., your-username/study-website)

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 1: Create the Public Website Repository
Step 1: Create the Public Website Repository

records.content:
Go to GitHub and create a new repository.

Name it appropriately (e.g. tambi-website).

Do not initialize it with a README, .gitignore, or license. Leave it completely empty.
Your workflow needs two secrets to function: one for the website password, and one to grant permission to push to the public repository.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 2: Create a Personal Access Token (PAT)
Step 2: Create a Personal Access Token (PAT)

records.content:
Because the workflow pushes code from your source repo to a different repository, the default GITHUB_TOKEN isn’t enough. You need a PAT.

Go to GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic).

Click Generate new token (classic).

Give it a name (e.g., Deploy Docs Token).

Under scopes, check repo (Full control of private repositories).

Click Generate token and copy the token immediately (you won’t see it again).

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 3: Add Secrets to the Source Repository
Step 3: Add Secrets to the Source Repository

records.content:
Go to your Source Repo (e.g. tambi_documentation).

Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.

Click New repository secret.

Name: DEPLOY_TOKEN

Value: Paste the PAT you just created.

Click Add secret.

Click New repository secret again.

Name: STATICRYPT_PASSWORD

Value: Choose the password you want visitors to type to access the website.

Click Add secret.
Now you’ll create the automated GitHub Actions workflow in your source repository.

In your source repo, create a file at .github/workflows/build-and-encrypt.yml.

Paste the following code into it:name: Build and Encrypt Site

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout Private Source Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install MyST and Staticrypt
        run: npm install -g mystmd staticrypt

      - name: Build MyST Site
        env:
          BASE_URL: /tambi-website/ # ⚠️ CHANGE THIS to match your public repo name!
        run: myst build --html

      - name: Scrub Source Files and Service Worker
        run: |
          echo "Deleting Service Worker..."
          rm -f ./_build/html/service-worker.js

          echo "Finding and deleting source Markdown files..."
          find ./_build/html -name "*.md" -type f -print -delete

          echo "Finding and deleting Notebook files..."
          find ./_build/html -name "*.ipynb" -type f -print -delete

          echo "Verification — any .md files remaining?"
          REMAINING=$(find ./_build/html -name "*.md" -type f)
          if [ -n "$REMAINING" ]; then
            echo "❌ WARNING: .md files still exist:"
            echo "$REMAINING"
          else
            echo "✅ No .md files remaining."
          fi

      - name: Encrypt HTML Files
        env:
          STATICRYPT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STATICRYPT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "${STATICRYPT_PASSWORD}" ]; then
            echo "❌ STATICRYPT_PASSWORD is EMPTY! Check your secret name."
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "✅ Password is set (length: ${#STATICRYPT_PASSWORD})"

          echo "Starting encryption..."
          FAILED=0
          while read -r file; do
            # Create a unique temp directory for this file's output
            TMPDIR=$(mktemp -d)

            # Encrypt the file — output goes to $TMPDIR/<filename>
            # Note: staticrypt v3 does not have an -o flag, must use -d
            if ! staticrypt "$file" -p "${STATICRYPT_PASSWORD}" -d "$TMPDIR"; then
              echo "❌ staticrypt failed for: $file"
              FAILED=1
              rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
              continue
            fi

            # Find the encrypted output file
            ENCRYPTED_FILE="$TMPDIR/$(basename "$file")"

            if [ -f "$ENCRYPTED_FILE" ]; then
              # Overwrite the original with the encrypted version
              cp "$ENCRYPTED_FILE" "$file"
              echo "✅ Encrypted: $file"
            else
              echo "❌ Encrypted file not found for: $file"
              FAILED=1
            fi

            rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
          done < <(find ./_build/html -name "*.html")

          if [ "$FAILED" -eq 1 ]; then
            echo "Encryption FAILED for one or more files."
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "Encryption complete."

      - name: Final Verification Before Deploy
        run: |
          echo "=== Checking for leaked source files ==="
          LEAKED=false

          MD_FILES=$(find ./_build/html -name "*.md" -type f)
          if [ -n "$MD_FILES" ]; then
            echo "❌ .md files found:"
            echo "$MD_FILES"
            LEAKED=true
          fi

          IPYNB_FILES=$(find ./_build/html -name "*.ipynb" -type f)
          if [ -n "$IPYNB_FILES" ]; then
            echo "❌ .ipynb files found:"
            echo "$IPYNB_FILES"
            LEAKED=true
          fi

          if [ "$LEAKED" = true ]; then
            echo "❌ Source files would be leaked! Aborting deploy."
            exit 1
          else
            echo "✅ No source files found. Safe to deploy."
          fi

          echo "=== Checking encryption ==="
          if head -n 5 ./_build/html/index.html | grep -qi "staticrypt"; then
            echo "✅ index.html is encrypted."
          else
            echo "❌ index.html is NOT encrypted!"
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Deploy to Public Repo
        uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
        with:
          publish_dir: ./_build/html
          external_repository: your-username/tambi-website # ⚠️ CHANGE THIS to your public repo!
          publish_branch: main
          personal_token: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
          force_orphan: true

⚠️ Make two changes in the file:

Change BASE_URL: /tambi-website/ to match your public repository name (e.g., /my-docs-site/).

Change external_repository: your-username/tambi-website to the full name of your public repository.

Commit the file to the main branch.

Go to your Public Website Repository (e.g., tambi-website).

Go to Settings → Pages.

Under “Build and deployment”, set Source to Deploy from a branch.

Set Branch to main and folder to / (root).

Click Save.

Make a small change to your source repository (like adding a space to a markdown file) and push it to main (git push origin main).

Go to the Actions tab in your source repository.

Watch the workflow run. It should pass all checks, including the ✅ No source files found and ✅ index.html is encrypted steps.

Once complete, go to https://your-username.github.io/tambi-website/ (replace with your repo name).

You should be greeted by a StatiCrypt password prompt! Enter the password you set in the STATICRYPT_PASSWORD secret to view your documentation.

You’re done! Now, every time you push changes to your private source repository, GitHub Actions will automatically build it, scrub the source files, encrypt the HTML, and deploy the secure version to your public website.

This chapter lists every step that leads from the raw files to the results reported in this documentation, in the order in which the steps have to be run. It replaces the working file how_to_run_this.md. Each step names the script, the folder it is run from, the command, its inputs and its outputs. Scripts that are no longer part of the pipeline are listed in 

the last section together with the reason, so that the decision does not have to be taken again.

The chapter covers the analysis of participant data. Training the two neural networks (the model classifier and the posterior network) and validating them on simulated data is a separate, much longer computation that is only repeated when the model changes. It is described in 

Amortized Bayesian Inference and 

Model Comparison; the pipeline below assumes that the trained networks exist.



Figure 1:The analysis pipeline. Columns show the stages from raw files to outputs, rows the three data streams. Colours mark the language of a script. The figure is drawn by tools/fig_pipeline_flowchart.py and has to be updated together with this chapter.

Folders. All commands are run from the analysis folder tambi-analysis unless a step states bayes_flow/ as working folder. The raw results files are in results/, the questionnaire scores in questionnaires/q_results/questionnaire_scores.csv.

Run tag. Every run writes into folders that carry a tag of the form [day]_[month]. In the commands below the tag is written as <tag>. The results currently reported in this book carry the tag 12_10 (run of 12 October 2026 with the adopted model). All results of one run therefore share one tag, and a result in this documentation can be traced to its run through the tag (see 

Book figures).

Shell. The commands are written for PowerShell on Windows; the backtick at the end of a line continues the command. R scripts are called through the full path of Rscript.exe, abbreviated below as Rscript:$Rscript = "C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.1\bin\Rscript.exe"

Division of labour. Python constructs data sets and figures. All statistical inference is done in R (lme4, lmerTest, glmmTMB, emmeans). A Python script that computes p-values is therefore either a model check or an interim solution, and is marked as such.

One command for the whole pipeline. Steps 3 to 10 can be run in order with tools/run_pipeline.ps1 (in the book folder). It calls the commands of this chapter, writes a log with the duration of every step to stats_results/<tag>/run_log.txt, and stops at the first error. Four scripts are not included and are run by hand when needed: h_switch_grid.py, within_state_diagnostics.py, parameter_behavior_models_v3.py and internalizing_state_analysis.py. The quality-control figures, the oddball diagnostics and the figure sync are included but are only run when they are named with -Steps.# show all steps
.\tools\run_pipeline.ps1 -List
# print the commands without running them
.\tools\run_pipeline.ps1 -Tag 08_10 -AnalysisRoot C:\path\to\tambi-analysis -DryRun
# run the core pipeline
.\tools\run_pipeline.ps1 -Tag 08_10 -AnalysisRoot C:\path\to\tambi-analysis
# run selected steps only
.\tools\run_pipeline.ps1 -Tag 08_10 -AnalysisRoot C:\path\to\tambi-analysis -Steps rq2,figs_rq2

Download all *_results.csv files from sciebo into tambi-analysis/results/.

Open RStudio and run helper_scripts/add_oddball_column_to_reults_file.R (the file name is spelled this way). The script adds the oddball flag to every results file in results/.

All later steps read the results files from results/. The former copy in bayes_flow/vp_results/ is no longer needed, because the scripts in bayes_flow/ are called with --results-dir ../results/. On 10 October 2026 both folders contained the same 68 files with identical checksums, so vp_results/ can be moved to the archive.

Log in to LimeSurvey, open Antworten, and choose Export, Antworten exportieren.

Select the output format Microsoft Excel (the csv export is faulty) and export questions as vollständiger Fragetext.

Save results-survey287866.xlsx in tambi-analysis/questionnaires/q_data/.

If a completed response has no SONA ID in the export (participants who opened the survey through the general link instead of the SONA link), add one row for it to questionnaires/q_data/sona_id_map.csv: the LimeSurvey response ID (Antwort ID), the SONA ID, and a note. The exported file itself is not edited.

Open RStudio and run questionnaires/q_analysis/questionnaire_scoring_pipeline.R completely, including section 12, which saves the results.

The output is questionnaires/q_results/questionnaire_scores.csv with one row per participant. All later steps read this file from this location; it is no longer copied to bayes_flow/q_results/.

The ID mapping file. sona_id_map.csv has the columns limesurvey_id, sona_id and note. The scoring script reads it after the export and uses the SONA ID of the file for every response that is listed. It prints how many IDs were filled in, confirmed or replaced, and it lists the LimeSurvey IDs of completed responses that still have no ID, so that missing entries are noticed at every run. The file was initialised on 10 October 2026 with the 160 pairs of the hand-completed export of 17 September 2026. In that export, 9 completed responses have no ID. The change to the scoring script was written without access to R and has to be confirmed at the next run.

python participant_analysis.py --data_dir results/ --out_dir participant_figures/<tag>/

The script draws the figures per participant, among them the net-placement heatmaps. They serve to check single participants and as example figures. They are not part of the statistical analysis.

python tambi_preprocessing.py `
    --data_dir results/ `
    --out_dir stats_results/<tag>/preprocessing/ `
    --window_post 3 `
    --exclude_second_post_event

Reads the results files and builds the tables for all later models, among them trial_level_dataset.csv and episode_level_dataset.csv. The construction of the tables is described in 

Dataset Construction.

python tambi_exploration.py `
    --data_dir stats_results/<tag>/preprocessing/ `
    --out_dir stats_results/<tag>/explore/ `
    --theme light

Descriptive figures of the raw data and summary tables. No tests.

& $Rscript tambi_main_models.R `
    --data_dir stats_results/<tag>/preprocessing/ `
    --out_dir  stats_results/<tag>/models/ `
    --power_nsim 200

Fits the mixed models for the effect of the instruction condition (M1, M3, M4a, M5, M7) and writes, for each model, the fixed effects, the estimated marginal means per condition, the planned contrasts and the diagnostics, together with rq1_results.txt. With --power_nsim the power analysis of tambi_power_analysis.R is run for the fitted models; without it the power analysis is skipped. The earlier argument --questionnaires has been removed from the command, because the script does not use it: all questionnaire models are in step 4.6.

Known issues of the power analysis

Model M3 is silently left out of the power analysis, because fit_M3 returns a list and the list is passed on where the fitted model is expected. The call has to pass m3$beta.

The power analysis covers the RQ1 models only. No RQ2 model is included yet.

Both points are open; see the to-do list on the 

front page.

python structural_signatures.py `
    --results_dir results/ `
    --out_dir stats_results/<tag>/structural_signatures `
    --cue_offset learned `
    --questionnaire_csv questionnaires/q_results/questionnaire_scores.csv

Reads the results files directly, so that every measure can be referred to the hidden-state target, and writes the event windows around transitions and oddballs (event_windows.csv), the trial pairs for the weighting of state error against outcome noise (selectivity_pairs.csv), the transfer episodes, and the participant-level measures. --cue_offset fixed uses the nominal offset of 70° instead of the offset each participant has learned and serves as a sensitivity analysis. --include_ids stats_results/<tag>/preprocessing/trial_level_dataset.csv restricts the analysis to the participants of step 4.1.

& $Rscript tambi_structural_signature_models.R `
    --windows stats_results/<tag>/structural_signatures/event_windows_with_traits.csv `
    --selectivity stats_results/<tag>/structural_signatures/selectivity_pairs_with_traits.csv `
    --out_dir stats_results/<tag>/structural_signature_models

& $Rscript tambi_rq2_models.R `
    --data_dir stats_results/<tag>/preprocessing `
    --windows stats_results/<tag>/structural_signatures/event_windows.csv `
    --pairs stats_results/<tag>/structural_signatures/selectivity_pairs.csv `
    --questionnaires questionnaires/q_results/questionnaire_scores.csv `
    --out_dir stats_results/<tag>/rq2_models

Fits models A to D separately for each of the five focal questionnaires (STICSA state, STICSA trait, IU, BDI, OCI), with the Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the five questionnaires for each focal term. The results are in rq2_results.txt, the full model summaries in rq2_model_summaries.txt, and the corrected focal tests in rq2_focal_tests_fdr.csv. --sections B,C fits a subset.

The analyses that were tried and excluded from the report are kept in tambi_excluded_models.R, together with a registry that states for each model what it measured and why it was excluded. The file has no command-line interface. It is sourced in R after the main script: source("tambi_main_models.R"); source("tambi_excluded_models.R"); run_excluded_models(data_dir, out_dir).
